EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
For a precise clock time, complete the sentence:


The overnight maintenance window begins ___ midnight and ends at 3:30 a.m.
column3:
The overnight maintenance window begins at midnight and ends at 3:30 a.m.


Use at for a precise time point, including noon and midnight.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose at night or during the night.


1. The observatory is open to visitors ___ . (the usual nightly period)
2. I woke twice ___ before the interview. (within that particular night)
column3:
1. The observatory is open to visitors at night.
2. I woke twice during the night before the interview.


Use at night for the normal general period. In contemporary AmE,
during the night is the natural production choice for an event within one
particular night.


Also OK in limited contexts: in the night, especially when the particular
night is already established.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2: Complete the fixed frame: at the ___ = now.
column3:
at the moment


At the moment means “now” in neutral conversation; keep the in this
fixed expression.


- The clinic cannot accept new patients at the moment.
- Fuel prices are relatively stable at the moment.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Maya became the youngest department head in the university's history ___ the
age of thirty-two.
column3:
Maya became the youngest department head in the university's history **at the
age of thirty-two**.


Use at the age of + number for an exact point in a person's life. Compare
in her thirties for the broader decade.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Complete with on or zero:


The revised accessibility standards take effect ___ Monday, September 16.
column3:
The revised accessibility standards take effect on Monday, September 16.


Use on with a named day or calendar date.


Also OK in AmE: takes effect Monday, September 16.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose on or in.


1. The advisory panel will release its findings ___ Thursday afternoon.
2. I generally do difficult analytical work ___ the afternoon.
column3:
1. The advisory panel will release its findings on Thursday afternoon.
2. I generally do difficult analytical work in the afternoon.


Use on + named day + morning/afternoon/evening for a particular day part.
Use in the afternoon when no named day narrows the period.


Also OK in AmE for 1: release its findings Thursday afternoon.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Complete the AmE weekend frames with on or zero.


1. We plan to migrate the database ___ the weekend.
2. We usually schedule major migrations ___ weekends.
column3:
1. We plan to migrate the database on the weekend.
2. We usually schedule major migrations on weekends.


Contemporary AmE normally uses on the weekend/on weekends.


Also OK for 1 when the whole period is foregrounded: over the weekend or
during the weekend. Chiefly BrE: at the weekend.


Also OK for 2 in AmE: schedule major migrations weekends.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose in or by. The intended meaning is “at some point during that
month,” not “by that October deadline.”


The city expects to complete the coastal resilience study ___ October 2027.
column3:
The city expects to complete the coastal resilience study in October 2027.


Use in with a month, year, or season. Use on for a specific date.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose in or for.


1. The replacement sensors will arrive ___ two weeks. (two weeks from now)
2. The field team will remain in Alaska ___ two weeks. (length of stay)
column3:
1. The replacement sensors will arrive in two weeks.
2. The field team will remain in Alaska for two weeks.


Use in + duration for when a future event will occur. Use **for +
duration** for how long an activity or state lasts.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Fix if wrong:


The research ethics committee will reconsider the application in next week.
column3:
The research ethics committee will reconsider the application next week.


Use no preposition before last, next, this, or every + time word:
last Monday, this quarter, every summer.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose during or for. The blank locates the interruption within the
event; it does not state its duration.


Several participants lost their internet connection ___ the webinar.
column3:
Several participants lost their internet connection during the webinar.


Use during + noun phrase for an event or bounded period. A finite-clause
linker such as while + subject + verb is a separate Module 05 decision.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose over or during. Which form foregrounds the six months as the
span across which a trend developed?


Public confidence improved steadily ___ the following six months.
column3:
Public confidence improved steadily over the following six months.


Use over + period for change, development, or repeated activity spread
across that period. During can locate an event within a period but does
not itself foreground development across the span.


Also OK in the printed sentence: during the following six months.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose throughout or during by meaning.


1. Emergency staff remained on duty ___ the entire storm. (at every stage)
2. Two brief power failures occurred ___ the storm. (at unspecified points)
column3:
1. Emergency staff remained on duty throughout the entire storm.
2. Two brief power failures occurred during the storm.


Throughout means during all parts of a period. During places something
within the period without claiming that it continued for all of it.


Also OK for 1: during the entire storm; entire itself supplies the
whole-period meaning.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
1. The laboratory has used renewable electricity ___ 2022. (starting point)
2. The laboratory has used renewable electricity ___ three years. (duration)
column3:
1. The laboratory has used renewable electricity since 2022.
2. The laboratory has used renewable electricity for three years.


Use since + starting point and for + duration, commonly with the
present perfect when the situation continues to now.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Complete the internal connection:


from + start ___ + end
column3:
from + start to + end


Use from + start + to + end for a complete range.


- The community health center is open from 8:00 a.m. to 6:00 p.m.
- Applications increased from 240 to 315 in one year.


Also OK in suitable ranges: between 8:00 a.m. and 6:00 p.m. and **from
8:00 a.m. until 6:00 p.m.**

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
1. Please submit the revised risk assessment ___ 5:00 p.m. (deadline)
2. A compliance officer will remain available ___ 5:00 p.m. (continuation)
column3:
1. Please submit the revised risk assessment by 5:00 p.m.
2. A compliance officer will remain available until 5:00 p.m.


By means no later than the deadline; completion may be earlier. Until
means an action or state continues up to the endpoint.


Also OK for 1 with the stricter meaning “earlier than 5:00”: **before 5:00
p.m.**

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose through or until.


1. The exhibition will remain open ___ Sunday. (Sunday is included)
2. The exhibition will remain open ___ Sunday morning. (closing endpoint)
column3:
1. The exhibition will remain open through Sunday.
2. The exhibition will remain open until Sunday morning.


In AmE, through + endpoint explicitly includes the endpoint. Until
marks continuation up to the stated stopping point.


Also OK for 1 with the same intended endpoint: throughout Sunday or
until the end of Sunday.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
1. The insurer must acknowledge the claim ___ five business days. (before the
limit expires)
2. The insurer will introduce its new portal ___ five business days. (five
days from now)
column3:
1. The insurer must acknowledge the claim within five business days.
2. The insurer will introduce its new portal in five business days.


Within + duration sets a time limit. In + duration predicts when a
future event will happen.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2: The municipality adopted its first heat-action plan ten years ___.
column3:
The municipality adopted its first heat-action plan ten years ago.


Place ago after a quantity of time to measure backward from now.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose before or after.


1. Back up the database ___ installing the security update.
2. Restart the service ___ completing the installation.
column3:
1. Back up the database before installing the security update.
2. Restart the service after completing the installation.


Use before/after + noun or V-ing to order events. A following verb takes
-ing because these words function as prepositions here.


Also OK as reformulations: prior to installing; **following completion
of** the installation.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose on time or in time.


1. The hearing began ___, exactly at its scheduled hour.
2. The attorney arrived just ___ to hear the opening statement.
column3:
1. The hearing began on time, exactly at its scheduled hour.
2. The attorney arrived just in time to hear the opening statement.


On time means at the scheduled time. In time means early enough for
something still to be possible.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2: Complete the fixed frame: from ___ to ___ = occasionally.
column3:
from time to time


From time to time is a neutral expression meaning “occasionally.”


- I still visit the regional office from time to time.
- The research team updates its coding guidelines from time to time.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose at or in.


1. A volunteer will meet you ___ the main entrance. (meeting point)
2. The orientation will take place ___ the auditorium. (inside the room)
column3:
1. A volunteer will meet you at the main entrance.
2. The orientation will take place in the auditorium.


Use at for a point or exact position and in for an enclosed area.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
1. The research institute is based ___ Vancouver.
2. Its reception desk is ___ 880 West Hastings Street.
column3:
1. The research institute is based in Vancouver.
2. Its reception desk is at 880 West Hastings Street.


Use in for the demonstrated city-scale area and at for a complete
numbered address or point.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose on or in.


1. The evacuation route is displayed ___ the wall beside the elevators.
2. Printed copies are stored ___ the cabinet below it.
column3:
1. The evacuation route is displayed on the wall beside the elevators.
2. Printed copies are stored in the cabinet below it.


Use on for contact with a surface and in for an enclosed space.


Also OK for 2 with a different viewpoint: inside the cabinet.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
1. Nora is working ___ home today. (ordinary location/activity)
2. The survey examined energy consumption ___ the home. (inside domestic
buildings as a setting)
column3:
1. Nora is working at home today.
2. The survey examined energy consumption in the home.


Use fixed at home without an article for ordinary location or activity.
Use in the home when treating the domestic interior as a setting or
category.


Also OK for 1: working from home, which foregrounds the remote-work
arrangement rather than simply the location.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2: at ___ = at the workplace or engaged in one's job
column3:
Use at work for being at the workplace or engaged in work. This fixed
institutional expression has no article.


- Priya is at work, but she can join the call after 4:00 p.m.
- Personal calls are discouraged at work.
- I concentrate more effectively at work than in a crowded café.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Which form foregrounds each named viewpoint: in school or at school?


1. Lina is still ___; she plans to graduate next year. (enrollment)
2. Lina is ___ now, helping with the science fair. (site/activity)
column3:
1. Lina is still in school; she plans to graduate next year.
2. Lina is at school now, helping with the science fair.


In AmE, in school commonly emphasizes enrollment or the period of
education; at school emphasizes presence or activity at the site.
Attendance contexts often permit either viewpoint.


Also OK when the other viewpoint is intended: at school can describe an
enrolled student's attendance, and in school can describe participation
in schooling.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Which form foregrounds the named viewpoint: at or in?


1. I cannot access the secure server remotely; I need to be ___ the office.
(workplace as the required site)
2. The package is ___ the office, on the shelf behind my desk. (literal
interior)
column3:
1. I need to be at the office.
2. The package is in the office, on the shelf behind my desk.


At the office presents it as a workplace or site; in the office
foregrounds the physical interior. In ordinary presence contexts, both can be
natural because the viewpoints overlap.


Also OK when the viewpoint changes: in the office for 1 and **at the
office** for 2 are both grammatical in ordinary AmE.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose at or in.


1. I met the new policy director ___ a public-health conference. (event)
2. I met her again ___ the conference room on the third floor. (room interior)
column3:
1. I met the new policy director at a public-health conference.
2. I met her again in the conference room on the third floor.


Use at + event for attendance and in + room for the physical interior.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
1. We reviewed the briefing notes ___ the train to Boston. (ordinary passenger
viewpoint)
2. The confidential folder is still ___ the rental car. (small private
vehicle)
column3:
1. We reviewed the briefing notes on the train to Boston.
2. The confidential folder is still in the rental car.


Use on by default for a passenger on a bus, train, or plane, and in for
a car or taxi. In a bus/train/plane is also possible when its physical
interior is specifically salient.


Also OK for 1 when the physical interior is salient: in the train.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose on or in for the conventional digital-location viewpoint.


1. The application form is available ___ the agency's website.
2. The eligibility criteria are explained ___ the guidance document.
column3:
1. The application form is available on the agency's website.
2. The eligibility criteria are explained in the guidance document.


Use on for a website, page, or platform; use in for content inside a
document, message, or chat.


Also OK as different constructions: via/through the website for access,
and within the guidance document for internal location.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose above or over. Which foregrounds neutral higher position, and
which foregrounds covering/alignment?


1. The emergency exit sign is ___ the doorway, at a higher position.
2. A protective canopy extends ___ the doorway and covers the entrance.
column3:
1. The emergency exit sign is above the doorway.
2. A protective canopy extends over the doorway and covers the entrance.


Above is neutral for a higher position. Over often adds direct
alignment, covering, or movement. For many ordinary higher-position
descriptions, above and over overlap.


Also OK for 1 in ordinary location contexts: over the doorway.
Also OK for 2: above the doorway; over more directly foregrounds the
canopy's covering and alignment with the entrance.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose below or under. Which fits a scale, and which foregrounds direct
vertical alignment?


1. The temperature fell ___ freezing, to a lower level on the scale.
2. The emergency supplies are stored ___ the stage, directly beneath it.
column3:
1. The temperature fell below freezing.
2. The emergency supplies are stored under the stage.


Below is neutral for a lower position or level. Under often adds
direct alignment, covering, or control. In many ordinary spatial contexts,
the two overlap.


Also OK for 2: below the stage or beneath the stage.


Also OK for 1 in limited AmE measurement talk: under freezing. **Below
freezing** is the neutral scale default.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose between or among.


1. The negotiator moved ___ the three delegations, treating each as a distinct
party.
2. The proposal generated concern ___ local business owners as a group.
column3:
1. The negotiator moved between the three delegations.
2. The proposal generated concern among local business owners.


Use between for distinct, separately identified items—even more than two.
Use among for membership or distribution within a group.


Also OK for 1 if the delegations are treated collectively rather than as
separate parties: among the three delegations.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose beside or near for the intended degree of proximity.


1. An interpreter sat directly ___ the witness throughout the hearing.
2. Several affordable hotels are ___ the convention center, within a
ten-minute walk.
column3:
1. An interpreter sat directly beside the witness.
2. Several affordable hotels are near the convention center.


Beside means directly next to. Near means generally close to.


Also OK for 1: next to or adjacent to. Also OK for 2: close to.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
The new legal-aid clinic is directly ___ the county courthouse, on the other
side of the street.
column3:
The new legal-aid clinic is directly opposite the county courthouse, on
the other side of the street.


Use opposite + place for a position facing it across a space.


Also OK: across from the county courthouse is the common AmE alternative.
Also OK: facing the county courthouse.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose in front of or behind for the intended opposite positions:


The press area is ___ the stage, while the technical crew works ___ it.
column3:
The press area is in front of the stage, while the technical crew works
behind it.


Use in front of and behind for opposite positions relative to another
object or place.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose inside or outside.


1. All medical equipment must remain ___ the marked sterile zone.
2. Visitors must wait ___ the marked sterile zone.
column3:
1. All medical equipment must remain inside the marked sterile zone.
2. Visitors must wait outside the marked sterile zone.


Use inside/outside + boundary for static location within or beyond that
boundary. Use into/out of when movement across it is the lesson.


Also OK for 1: within the marked sterile zone.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose inside or beyond. The intended location is farther than the
boundary, not within it.


Mobile service becomes unreliable ___ the northern boundary of the national
park.
column3:
Mobile service becomes unreliable **beyond the northern boundary of the
national park**.


Use beyond + boundary for a place farther than that boundary or limit.


Also OK as sentence-level alternatives: past or outside the northern
boundary.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose at or in for the target fixed frames.


1. A small monitoring station stands ___ the edge of the wetland.
2. A protected nesting area lies ___ the center of the wetland.
column3:
1. A small monitoring station stands at the edge of the wetland.
2. A protected nesting area lies in the center of the wetland.


Use at the edge for a peripheral point and in the center for a central
area within something.


Also OK with different spatial precision: on/near the edge and **in the
middle**.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose to or toward by the intended meaning.


1. The delegation traveled ___ Geneva for the negotiations. (destination)
2. The protesters moved ___ the embassy but stopped two blocks away.
(direction only)
column3:
1. The delegation traveled to Geneva for the negotiations.
2. The protesters moved toward the embassy but stopped two blocks away.


To presents a destination, though arrival is not guaranteed by every verb.
Toward gives direction without presenting the place as the destination
reached.


Also OK for 2: towards the embassy. Toward is the preferred AmE
spelling.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Fix if wrong:


After the emergency drill, employees were allowed to go to home early.
column3:
After the emergency drill, employees were allowed to go home early.


When home is a destination adverb, use go/come/arrive + home without
to.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Fix if wrong:


Please bring the signed consent forms to here before the afternoon session.
column3:
Please bring the signed consent forms here before the afternoon session.


Directional adverbs such as here, there, upstairs, and downstairs
normally follow movement verbs without to.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
1. The visiting scholars arrived ___ Seoul on Sunday evening.
2. They arrived ___ the conference venue shortly before registration closed.
column3:
1. The visiting scholars arrived in Seoul.
2. They arrived at the conference venue.


Use arrive in for a city, country, or large area and arrive at for a
point or venue. Say arrive home with no preposition.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2: The overnight train departs ___ Union Station at 10:15 p.m.
column3:
The overnight train departs from Union Station at 10:15 p.m.


Use from + source to identify the starting location of movement.


Also OK in formal transport style: departs Union Station.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose out of or off.


1. The technician lifted the damaged battery ___ its protective case.
2. She then lifted the case ___ the workbench.
column3:
1. The technician lifted the damaged battery out of its protective case.
2. She then lifted the case off the workbench.


Use out of for movement from inside an enclosure and off for movement
away from a surface.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose into or in.


1. From the corridor, the inspection team walked ___ the restricted
laboratory. (boundary crossing)
2. The inspection team is now ___ the restricted laboratory. (location)
column3:
1. From the corridor, the inspection team walked **into the restricted
laboratory**.
2. The inspection team is now in the restricted laboratory.


Use into for movement ending inside an enclosed place; use in for
static location.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose onto or on for the target movement-versus-location contrast.


1. The presenter stepped ___ the platform. (movement to the surface)
2. She remained ___ the platform during the discussion. (location)
column3:
1. The presenter stepped onto the platform.
2. She remained on the platform during the discussion.


Use onto for movement ending on a surface and on for static location.


Also OK for 1 in ordinary movement contexts: stepped on the platform.
Onto makes the endpoint movement more explicit.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose across or through. The first path runs from the west side to the
east side of an open plaza; the second enters and passes within a covered
passage.


1. Residents walked ___ the open plaza to reach the shelter.
2. They continued ___ a covered passage beneath the highway.
column3:
1. Residents walked across the open plaza.
2. They continued through a covered passage beneath the highway.


Use across from one side of an area or surface to the other. Use
through for a path within an enclosed or three-dimensional space.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose along or past. The canal is the route being followed, not a
landmark left behind.


Follow the riverside path ___ the canal until you reach the pedestrian bridge.
column3:
Follow the riverside path along the canal until you reach the pedestrian
bridge.


Use along + route for movement following the length or course of a road,
river, path, or boundary.


Also OK as different location descriptions, not the route-following frame:
beside/alongside the canal.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose along or past. The library is a landmark left behind, not the
route being followed.


Continue ___ the municipal library; the legal-aid office is the next building.
column3:
Continue past the municipal library; the legal-aid office is the next
building.


Use past + landmark for movement beyond a point without treating that
landmark as the route.


Also OK as sentence-level alternatives: beyond/by the municipal library.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose around or past. The route curves to avoid the barrier rather
than treating it as a landmark on an unobstructed path.


Because the central staircase was blocked, visitors had to walk ___ the
construction barrier to reach the elevators.
column3:
Because the central staircase was blocked, visitors had to walk **around the
construction barrier** to reach the elevators.


Use around + obstacle for a path that avoids or curves around it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose around or toward. The tour moves among several parts of the
campus and has no single endpoint.


During orientation, student ambassadors guided us ___ the campus to see the
library, laboratories, and health center.
column3:
During orientation, student ambassadors guided us around the campus to see
the library, laboratories, and health center.


Use move/travel around + area for movement among several parts without one
single endpoint.


Also OK with different path construals: through/across the campus.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose over or under for a crossing path.


1. The drone crossed ___ the flooded road. (above it)
2. The maintenance crew crossed ___ the raised fence panel. (below it)
column3:
1. The drone crossed over the flooded road.
2. The maintenance crew crossed under the raised fence panel.


Use over/under + obstacle for a movement path above or below it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose by or with. One blank names the agent; the other names the
physical instrument.


The encrypted archive was opened ___ an external auditor ___ a temporary
access key.
column3:
The encrypted archive was opened **by an external auditor with a temporary
access key**.


In a passive clause, by names the agent performing the action; with
names the physical instrument used.


Also OK as a reformulation: using a temporary access key.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose the structures by + V-ing or with + instrument.


1. The team reduced processing time ___ automating routine checks. (method)
2. The team opened the damaged casing ___ a specialized tool. (instrument)
column3:
1. The team reduced processing time by automating routine checks.
2. The team opened the damaged casing with a specialized tool.


Use by + V-ing for the method used to achieve a result. Use **with + noun
phrase** for a physical instrument.


Also OK as sentence-level reformulations: **through automating routine
checks; using a specialized tool**.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose via or on. The sentence names the channel by which updates are
delivered, not the place where they appear.


Applicants will receive interview updates ___ the university's secure
messaging portal.
column3:
Applicants will receive interview updates **via the university's secure
messaging portal**.


Use via + channel, intermediary, or route to show how something is
transmitted or routed.


Also OK in the printed sentence: **through/using the university's secure
messaging portal**.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose from for a source/cause and through for a sustained process.


1. Prolonged hearing loss can develop ___ repeated exposure to industrial
noise. (source/cause)
2. The coalition built public support ___ months of consultation, revision,
and outreach. (sustained process)
column3:
1. Prolonged hearing loss can develop **from repeated exposure to industrial
noise**.
2. The coalition built public support **through months of consultation,
revision, and outreach**.


Use from + source/cause to identify what a result arises from. Use
through + process to foreground the sustained means by which an outcome
develops. These are meaning choices, not categorical exclusions.


Also OK with a different construal: because of/due to repeated exposure;
by/after/following months of consultation.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose for + V-ing or to + base verb.


1. This dashboard is ___ monitoring real-time energy use. (the thing's
function)
2. Analysts open the dashboard ___ identify unusual demand patterns. (their
purpose in acting)
column3:
1. This dashboard is for monitoring real-time energy use.
2. Analysts open the dashboard to identify unusual demand patterns.


The requested constructions present a thing's function with for + V-ing
and an agent's purpose in acting with to + base verb. These are useful
tendencies, not exclusive licensing rules.


Also OK as a reformulation of 1: **This dashboard is to monitor real-time
energy use.**

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose for or to.


1. The city created a free legal-advice service ___ low-income tenants.
(intended beneficiaries)
2. The city sent the revised guidance ___ every registered landlord.
(transfer recipient)
column3:
1. The city created a free legal-advice service for low-income tenants.
2. The city sent the revised guidance to every registered landlord.


Use for for the person or group intended to benefit. Use to for the
recipient of a transfer.


Also OK as a purpose-clause reformulation of 1: **The city created a free
legal-advice service to support low-income tenants.**

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose about or on. Which is the broad neutral default, and which
foregrounds a focused/formal presentation?


1. We had an informal conversation ___ workplace flexibility.
2. The professor delivered a focused lecture ___ algorithmic bias in hiring.
column3:
1. We had an informal conversation about workplace flexibility.
2. The professor delivered a focused lecture **on algorithmic bias in
hiring**.


About is the broad neutral default. On is common for focused,
issue-centered, or more formal material. The two overlap substantially.


Also OK for 1: a conversation on workplace flexibility in a focused
discussion. Also OK for 2: a lecture about algorithmic bias.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Complete with like or unlike.


1. The revised plan is ___ the earlier proposal: both protect temporary
workers.
2. The revised plan is ___ the earlier proposal: only the revision includes an
appeals process.
column3:
1. The revised plan is like the earlier proposal in that respect.
2. The revised plan is unlike the earlier proposal in that respect.


Use like + noun phrase for similarity and unlike + noun phrase for
difference. Use as, not like, when naming the role in which someone or
something functions.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Complete with as or like. Dr. Chen attended in the actual capacity of
an independent technical adviser, not merely in a similar manner.


Dr. Chen attended the negotiations ___ an independent technical adviser.
column3:
Dr. Chen attended the negotiations as an independent technical adviser.


Use as + role/function for the capacity in which someone or something
acts. Like an adviser would mean similarity, not that this was her actual
role.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose except or exception but. Use the neutral default in 1 and the
restricted/formal alternative after no in 2.


1. Every regional office ___ the coastal branch met the target.
2. No regional office ___ the coastal branch missed the target.
column3:
1. Every regional office except the coastal branch met the accessibility
target.
2. No regional office but the coastal branch missed the target.


Use except + noun phrase to exclude a member from a group. But can have
the same exception meaning after restrictive words such as no or none,
but is more restricted and formal.


Also OK for both printed sentences: except. Also OK for 1, though less
usual in neutral AmE: exception but.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose of or from for the requested material construal.


1. The exhibition cases are made ___ solid aluminum. (basic material)
2. The acoustic panels are made ___ discarded textiles. (manufacturing source)
column3:
1. The exhibition cases are made of solid aluminum.
2. The acoustic panels are made from discarded textiles.


Use made of + basic material when naming what an object consists of. Use
made from + source material when foregrounding a manufacturing
transformation. This is a strong tendency, not an absolute visible/transformed
test.


Also OK in suitable manufacturing contexts: made from aluminum; **made of
textile fibers**.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Complete with by or zero:


After the insulation upgrade, the building's annual energy consumption fell
___ 18 percent.
column3:
After the insulation upgrade, the building's annual energy consumption fell
by 18 percent.


Use by + amount for the size of a change or difference.


Also OK: energy consumption fell 18 percent.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
1. The wildfire is now ___ control; firefighters have contained it.
2. The incident commander is ___ control of the evacuation.
column3:
1. The wildfire is now under control.
2. The incident commander is in control of the evacuation.


Under control describes something being controlled. In control of
describes the person or group exercising control.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2: Complete the fixed internal connection: in response ___ + trigger.
column3:
in response to + trigger


Use in response to + trigger for an action or reaction prompted by
something.


- The hospital expanded counseling services in response to rising demand.
- The city revised the route in response to residents' concerns.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Complete the fixed frame with both accepted prepositions:


in comparison ___/___ + comparator
column3:
in comparison with/to + comparator


Use in comparison with/to + comparator to introduce a formal comparison;
both prepositions are accepted.


- In comparison with last year, operating costs have fallen.
- The new material is lightweight in comparison to concrete.


Also OK as shorter sentence-level alternatives: compared with/to and
relative to.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Complete the fixed frame with both accepted prepositions:


in contrast ___/___ + comparator
column3:
in contrast to/with + comparator


Use in contrast to/with + comparator to mark a formal difference.


- In contrast to the national trend, local enrollment increased.
- This year's dry conditions stand in contrast with last year's floods.


Also OK as different sentence-level constructions: unlike, **compared
with, or despite**, when the intended relation supports them.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2: Complete the fixed internal connection: in accordance ___ + rule/agreement.
column3:
in accordance with + rule/agreement


Use formal in accordance with + rule/agreement for action that conforms to
that authority.


- Personal data must be deleted in accordance with the retention policy.
- The funds were distributed in accordance with the agreement.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2: Complete the fixed internal connection: in line ___ + policy/evidence.
column3:
in line with + policy/evidence


Use in line with + policy/evidence/expectation for consistency or
agreement.


- The emissions target is in line with current scientific advice.
- Salaries will increase in line with inflation.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose on behalf of or for. Use the delegated-representation phrase in
1 and the short neutral beneficiary phrase in 2.


1. The union president signed the agreement ___ all teaching assistants.
2. The university created an emergency fund ___ teaching assistants.
column3:
1. The union president signed the agreement **on behalf of all teaching
assistants**.
2. The university created an emergency fund for teaching assistants.


Use on behalf of for representation and for for an intended
beneficiary. On behalf of can also mean “for the benefit of,” so this is a
primary-use distinction, not an exclusive grammar rule.


Also OK for 1 when the representative meaning is clear: **signed the agreement
for all teaching assistants**.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2: Complete the fixed internal connection: on the basis ___ + grounds.
column3:
on the basis of + grounds


Use on the basis of + evidence/criteria for the grounds of a decision or
judgment.


- Applications were ranked on the basis of scientific merit.
- The regulator rejected the claim on the basis of insufficient evidence.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Complete the fixed internal connections.


1. in support ___ + proposal
2. in opposition ___ + proposal
column3:
1. in support of + proposal
2. in opposition to + proposal


Use in support of for a position favoring a proposal and **in opposition
to** for a position against it.


Shorter stance alternatives: for and against.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2: Complete the fixed internal connection: at risk ___ + V-ing/noun.
column3:
at risk of + V-ing/noun


Use at risk of + noun/V-ing for danger of an unwanted result.


- Several coastal homes are at risk of flooding.
- Without treatment, the patient is at risk of serious complications.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2: Complete the fixed internal connection: under pressure ___ + base verb.
column3:
under pressure to + base verb


Use under pressure to + base verb when someone is strongly urged or
compelled to act.


- The hospital is under pressure to reduce waiting times.
- Small businesses are under pressure to lower their prices.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Complete the Module 01 fixed frame:


in case ___ + noun phrase
column3:
in case of + noun phrase


Use in case of + noun phrase to mean “if or when the named event occurs,”
especially in instructions. The finite-clause construction **in case +
subject + verb** is a separate Module 05 decision.


- Use the stairs in case of fire.
- Call this number in case of an emergency.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2: Complete the fixed internal connection: in the absence ___ + person/thing.
column3:
in the absence of + person/thing


Use formal in the absence of + person/thing when it is not present or
available.


- In the absence of reliable evidence, the claim was rejected.
- The deputy will chair the meeting in the absence of the director.


Also OK as a sentence-level alternative: **without reliable clinical
evidence**.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Researchers must register the study protocol ___ collecting any participant
data.
column3:
Researchers must register the study protocol **in advance of collecting any
participant data**.


Use in advance of + event/V-ing for something done beforehand.


Also OK: before collecting any participant data is the less formal
alternative.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Fix if wrong:


The committee approved the pilot program without to review the independent
safety assessment.
column3:
The committee approved the pilot program **without reviewing the independent
safety assessment**.


When a verb follows a preposition such as without, use the V-ing form,
not a to-infinitive.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
1. Between you and ___, the proposed deadline is unrealistic. (speaker)
2. The final decision rests with the director and ___. (male colleague)
column3:
1. Between you and me, the proposed deadline is unrealistic.
2. The final decision rests with the director and him.


Use object pronouns after a preposition: me, him, her, us, them.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
The lexical frame is speak to. Put its preposition in the ordinary AmE and
formal positions.


1. Who did the external auditor speak ___ after the hearing?
2. ___ whom did the external auditor speak after the hearing?
column3:
1. Who did the external auditor speak to after the hearing?
2. To whom did the external auditor speak after the hearing?


Ordinary AmE commonly leaves the preposition at the end. Formal style may
place it before whom. The final preposition in sentence 1 is fully
grammatical.


Also OK with a different lexical frame: **Who did the auditor speak with? /
With whom did the auditor speak?**

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::01 Prepositions and Prepositional Phrases
column2:
Choose out or out of.


1. When the alarm sounds, go ___ immediately. (no object)
2. When the alarm sounds, go ___ the building through the nearest emergency
exit. (object: the building)
column3:
1. When the alarm sounds, go out immediately.
2. When the alarm sounds, go **out of the building through the nearest
emergency exit**.


Use directional adverb out without an object. Use prepositional **out of +
place** when naming the enclosure or boundary left.


Other words such as outside or away can express different directions;
the bounded choice here tests whether the printed form has an object.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
Please answer to the final question in the survey.
column3:
Please answer the final question in the survey.


As a verb, answer + question takes a direct object with no to.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
The committee discussed about the revised admissions policy.
column3:
The committee discussed the revised admissions policy.


Use discuss + topic, with no about. Compare: The committee talked about the policy.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
Visitors must show identification before they enter into the laboratory.
column3:
Visitors must show identification before they enter the laboratory.


For literal movement into a place, use enter + place, with no into.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
We should reach to the conference center before registration closes.
column3:
We should reach the conference center before registration closes.


Use reach + destination, with no to.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
The report mentions about several barriers to rural health care.
column3:
The report mentions several barriers to rural health care.


Use mention + topic, with no about. Compare: The report talks about several barriers.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
As the interview began, Maya approached to the reception desk.
column3:
As the interview began, Maya approached the reception desk.


In the literal movement sense, use approach + person/place, with no to.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
If the error persists, contact with the technical support team.
column3:
If the error persists, contact the technical support team.


The verb uses contact + person, with a direct object. The noun pattern is different: remain in contact with the team.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the briefing report with the required form of explain:


The analyst explained ___ ___ the board. (the issue; the recipient)
column3:
The analyst explained the issue to the board.


Use explain + thing + to + person. The thing is the direct object; a recipient is introduced by to. Do not use explain the board the issue.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the accountability statement with the required form of answer:


Senior executives must ___ any deliberate concealment of safety data.
column3:
Senior executives must answer for any deliberate concealment of safety data.


Answer for + action/consequence means be held responsible for it. This differs from answer + question.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete both accounts with describe:


1. The architect described ___ ___ the residents. (the design; the recipients)
2. The architect described ___ how the courtyard would be restored. (the recipients)
column3:
1. The architect described the design to the residents.
2. The architect described to the residents how the courtyard would be restored.


Use describe + thing + to + person. Do not use describe the residents the design.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
More than two hundred researchers attended at the symposium.
column3:
More than two hundred researchers attended the symposium.


For going to an event, use attend + event, with no at.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
After orientation, Priya joined the campus debate club.
column3:
Correct as written.


After orientation, Priya joined the campus debate club.


Use join + group with a direct object. Join in + activity is also valid in a different frame: She joined in the discussion.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the matched descriptions:


1. The prototype ___ the earlier model in several respects. (use resemble)
2. The prototype ___ the earlier model in several respects. (use look)
column3:
1. The prototype resembles the earlier model in several respects.
2. The prototype looks like the earlier model in several respects.


Use resemble + direct object, with no to. The corresponding pattern is look like + object.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
Many small clinics lack of reliable internet access.
column3:
Many small clinics lack reliable internet access.


The verb uses lack + thing. The noun uses a lack of + thing.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the matched statements:


1. Several residents ___ the rezoning plan. (use oppose)
2. Several residents ___ the rezoning plan. (use object)
column3:
1. Several residents oppose the rezoning plan.
2. Several residents object to the rezoning plan.


Use oppose + direct object, but object to + noun/V-ing.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
The proposal fails to address to the shortage of affordable housing.
column3:
The proposal fails to address the shortage of affordable housing.


In the sense “deal with an issue,” use address + issue, with no to.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Express the same whole-to-parts relationship with comprise in active and passive form:


1. The curriculum ___ six core courses.
2. The curriculum ___ six core courses. (passive)
column3:
1. The curriculum comprises six core courses.
2. The curriculum is comprised of six core courses.


Active whole + comprise + parts and passive whole + be comprised of + parts are both established. Also natural: The curriculum is composed of six core courses.


Some readers still criticize be comprised of. When that criticism matters, be composed of is the safest passive alternative.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
Social expectations strongly influence on career choices.
column3:
Social expectations strongly influence career choices.


The verb uses influence + direct object. The noun uses influence on: Their influence on career choices is substantial.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the matched cause-and-result statements:


1. Prolonged noise can ___ sleep quality. (use the verb affect)
2. Prolonged noise can have a harmful ___ on sleep quality. (use the noun effect)
column3:
1. Prolonged noise can affect sleep quality.
2. Prolonged noise can have a harmful effect on sleep quality.


The verb is affect + direct object. The related noun is effect on + target.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the matched formal and neutral statements:


1. The research team ___ approval from the ethics board. (use await)
2. The research team ___ approval from the ethics board. (use wait)
column3:
1. The research team awaits approval from the ethics board.
2. The research team is waiting for approval from the ethics board.


Formal await + direct object takes no for. Neutral wait for + object requires for.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the matched formal and neutral requests:


1. The committee is ___ independent legal advice. (use seek)
2. The committee is ___ independent legal advice. (use look)
column3:
1. The committee is seeking independent legal advice.
2. The committee is looking for independent legal advice.


Formal seek + direct object takes no for. Look for + object includes the preposition.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the condition with the required form of depend:


Whether the trial continues will ___ the safety review.
column3:
Whether the trial continues will depend on the safety review.


Use depend on + thing/person for a condition or source of reliance. The preposition cannot be separated from depend.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the trust statement with the required form of rely:


Rural hospitals often ___ volunteer emergency responders.
column3:
Rural hospitals often rely on volunteer emergency responders.


Use rely on + thing/person for trust or dependence.


Also OK: rely upon volunteer emergency responders is more formal.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the support statement with the required form of count:


During the transition, new staff can ___ their mentors for practical guidance.
column3:
During the transition, new staff can count on their mentors for practical guidance.


Here, count on + person/thing means expect reliable support.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the cause statement with the required form of contribute:


Chronic sleep deprivation can ___ impaired judgment.
column3:
Chronic sleep deprivation can contribute to impaired judgment.


Use contribute to + result when something is one cause of that result.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete both directions of the causal relationship:


1. Inadequate maintenance can result ___ equipment failure.
2. The equipment failure resulted ___ inadequate maintenance.
column3:
1. Inadequate maintenance can result in equipment failure.
2. The equipment failure resulted from inadequate maintenance.


Result in + effect points toward an outcome. Result from + cause points back to its source.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the source statement with the required form of stem:


Much of the disagreement ___ different assumptions about risk.
column3:
Much of the disagreement stems from different assumptions about risk.


Formal stem from + source means originate in that source.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Read the two completed verb frames. Are both established in contemporary AmE, and which is usually more concise in edited prose?


1. The new zoning rules may impact small businesses directly.
2. The new zoning rules may impact on small businesses.
column3:
Both verb frames are established:


1. transitive impact + target
2. intransitive impact on + target


The direct-object frame is usually more concise in edited AmE.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the two senses of account for:


1. A change in reporting rules may ___ the apparent increase.
2. Online sales now ___ nearly half of total revenue.
column3:
1. A change in reporting rules may account for the apparent increase.
2. Online sales now account for nearly half of total revenue.


Account for + fact means explain it. Account for + share means constitute that proportion.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the activity statement with the required form of participate:


All first-year students must ___ a community research project.
column3:
All first-year students must participate in a community research project.


Use participate in + activity to mean take part in it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the activity statement with the required form of engage:


The course asks students to ___ sustained independent research.
column3:
The course asks students to engage in sustained independent research.


Use engage in + activity for active participation. Engage with has other meanings, such as interacting with an audience or idea.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the attention statement with the required form of focus:


This briefing will ___ the policy's long-term fiscal effects.
column3:
This briefing will focus on the policy's long-term fiscal effects.


Use focus on + topic to direct attention to that topic.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the task statement with the required form of concentrate:


Please ___ verifying the figures before revising the conclusion.
column3:
Please concentrate on verifying the figures before revising the conclusion.


Use concentrate on + noun/V-ing for the task receiving full attention.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the two roles in one application:


Nora applied ___ the National Science Foundation ___ a research fellowship.
column3:
Nora applied to the National Science Foundation for a research fellowship.


Use apply to + organization + for + thing requested.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the purchase statement with the required form of pay:


The grant will ___ specialized laboratory equipment.
column3:
The grant will pay for specialized laboratory equipment.


Use pay for + thing/service for what money purchases. A recipient can be direct: The university paid the supplier.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the investment statement with the required form of invest:


The city plans to ___ flood-resistant infrastructure.
column3:
The city plans to invest in flood-resistant infrastructure.


Use invest in + asset/project for putting money, time, or effort into it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the two allocation statements with the required form of spend:


1. The agency spent $2 million ___ cybersecurity upgrades.
2. The agency spent six months ___ the new system. (use test)
column3:
1. The agency spent $2 million on cybersecurity upgrades.
2. The agency spent six months testing the new system.


Use spend + money/time + on + noun or spend + money/time + V-ing.


Also OK for 2: The agency spent six months on testing the new system. The zero form is more concise here.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the service-fee statement with the required form of charge:


The consultant charged the nonprofit $800 ___ the accessibility audit.
column3:
The consultant charged the nonprofit $800 for the accessibility audit.


Use charge + person + amount + for + service when asking someone to pay for a service.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the recipient and reason in one apology:


The editor apologized ___ the author ___ publishing the quotation without permission.
column3:
The editor apologized to the author for publishing the quotation without permission.


Use apologize to + person for the recipient and apologize for + noun/V-ing for the reason.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the shared-opinion statement with the required form of agree:


After reviewing the evidence, I ___ the independent auditor's conclusion.
column3:
After reviewing the evidence, I agree with the independent auditor's conclusion.


Use agree with + person/opinion when sharing a view or judging an opinion correct.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Choose the meaning of agreed on in this completed sentence:


After comparing four possible dates, both sides agreed on May 15.


Does agreed on mean jointly selected the date or accepted an offered proposal?
column3:
It means both sides jointly selected May 15.


Use agree on + decision/plan/date for a jointly reached choice. Use agree to + proposal/request/terms when accepting something offered.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the acceptance statement with the required form of agree:


The landlord offered a six-month extension, and the tenant ___ the proposal.
column3:
The landlord offered a six-month extension, and the tenant agreed to the proposal.


Use agree to + proposal/request/terms when accepting something offered. Compare agree to revise, where to begins an infinitive.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the topic and interlocutor in one disagreement:


The two researchers argued ___ data ownership ___ the department chair.
column3:
The two researchers argued about data ownership with the department chair.


Use argue about/over + topic and argue with + person.


Also OK: The two researchers argued over data ownership with the department chair.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the message-response statement with the required form of reply:


The admissions office has not yet ___ my request for clarification.
column3:
The admissions office has not yet replied to my request for clarification.


Use reply to + message/person. Reply may also appear without an object, but a following target uses to.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the stimulus-response statement with the required form of respond:


Most patients ___ the new treatment within six weeks.
column3:
Most patients responded to the new treatment within six weeks.


Use respond to + stimulus for a reaction to something.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the purpose and recipient patterns:


1. The grant provides funding ___ tenant advocacy.
2. The grant provides tenant groups ___ funding.
column3:
1. The grant provides funding for tenant advocacy.
2. The grant provides tenant groups with funding.


Use provide + thing + for + purpose or provide + person + with + thing. Provide + thing + to + recipient is also grammatical, but it expresses a recipient rather than the purpose tested in sentence 1.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the harm-prevention statement with the required form of protect:


The new insulation protects the pipes ___ freezing.
column3:
The new insulation protects the pipes from freezing.


Use protect + person/thing + from + danger or unwanted result.


Also OK: protects the pipes against freezing is possible, especially when the danger is framed as a threat.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
The security update prevented attackers to access customer records.
column3:
The security update prevented attackers from accessing customer records.


Use prevent + person/thing + from + V-ing, not prevent + person + to-infinitive.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the difficulty-management statement with the required form of cope:


Many caregivers struggle to ___ prolonged uncertainty.
column3:
Many caregivers struggle to cope with prolonged uncertainty.


Use cope with + problem for managing a difficult situation.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the problem-management statement with the required form of deal:


The revised protocol explains how to ___ a suspected data breach.
column3:
The revised protocol explains how to deal with a suspected data breach.


Use deal with + problem/person for taking action concerning that problem or person.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the advantage statement with the required form of benefit:


Small exporters could ___ a simpler customs procedure.
column3:
Small exporters could benefit from a simpler customs procedure.


Use benefit from + thing for gaining an advantage from it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the illness statement with the required form of suffer:


Millions of adults ___ chronic sleep disorders.
column3:
Millions of adults suffer from chronic sleep disorders.


Use suffer from + illness/serious problem for experiencing that condition.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the return-to-normal statement with the required form of recover:


The local economy is still ___ last year's severe flooding.
column3:
The local economy is still recovering from last year's severe flooding.


Use recover from + illness/setback for returning to normal afterward.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the adjustment statement with the required form of adapt:


Coastal communities must ___ more frequent extreme weather.
column3:
Coastal communities must adapt to more frequent extreme weather.


Use adapt to + change for becoming suited to new conditions.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the document-reference statement with the required form of refer:


For eligibility details, please ___ Section 4 of the application guide.
column3:
For eligibility details, please refer to Section 4 of the application guide.


Use refer to + thing/person to mention it or direct attention to it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the impersonal connection statement with the required form of relate:


These findings directly ___ the debate over algorithmic bias.
column3:
These findings directly relate to the debate over algorithmic bias.


Here, relate to + topic/issue means be connected or relevant to it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the personal-identification statement with the required form of relate:


As a first-generation student, I could ___ the narrator's sense of isolation.
column3:
As a first-generation student, I could relate to the narrator's sense of isolation.


Here, relate to + person/experience means recognize one's own feelings or experience in it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the stimulus-response statement with the required form of react:


Financial markets ___ the unexpected rate increase within minutes.
column3:
Financial markets reacted to the unexpected rate increase within minutes.


Use react to + stimulus for showing a response to it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the opposition statement with the required form of object:


Several faculty members ___ replacing seminars with recorded lectures.
column3:
Several faculty members objected to replacing seminars with recorded lectures.


Use object to + noun/V-ing. Here to is a preposition, so a following action takes V-ing, not a base verb.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the deliberate-action and perception statements:


1. During the briefing, everyone ___ the safety officer carefully. (use listen)
2. From the hallway, I could ___ the safety officer clearly. (use hear)
column3:
1. During the briefing, everyone listened to the safety officer carefully.
2. From the hallway, I could hear the safety officer clearly.


Listen to + sound/person is deliberate attention. Hear + direct object is perception.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the visual-attention statement with the required form of look:


Please ___ the trend line in Figure 3.
column3:
Please look at the trend line in Figure 3.


Use look at + visual target for directing your eyes or attention toward it. Use look into + issue for an investigation.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the explicit search statement with the required form of look:


Investigators are ___ the missing maintenance records.
column3:
Investigators are looking for the missing maintenance records.


Use look for + search target to mean try to find it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the temporary-care statement with the required form of look:


Could you ___ my dog while I attend the conference?
column3:
Could you look after my dog while I attend the conference?


Use look after + dependent/person/property for taking care of it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the whole-to-parts statement with the required form of consist:


The assessment ___ a written report and a fifteen-minute presentation.
column3:
The assessment consists of a written report and a fifteen-minute presentation.


Use whole + consist of + parts. Also natural: The assessment is composed of a written report and a presentation. With comprise, reverse the grammar, not the relationship: The assessment comprises a report and a presentation.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the ownership statement with the required form of belong:


These confidential records ___ the hospital, not the contractor.
column3:
These confidential records belong to the hospital, not the contractor.


Use belong to + owner for ownership.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the professional-field statement with the required form of specialize:


The clinic ___ treating rare neurological disorders.
column3:
The clinic specializes in treating rare neurological disorders.


Use specialize in + field/noun/V-ing for a professional or academic focus.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the eligibility and ability statements:


1. Her income qualifies her ___ the housing subsidy.
2. Her certification qualifies her ___ inspect commercial buildings.
column3:
1. Her income qualifies her for the housing subsidy.
2. Her certification qualifies her to inspect commercial buildings.


Use qualify + person + for + position/benefit for eligibility and qualify + person + to + verb for authorized ability.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Read both completed comparisons. What usage tendency do with and to illustrate?


1. The study compares the new treatment with standard care.
2. The speaker compares urban growth to the spread of a living organism.
column3:
Both with and to are possible in both sentences.


Compare with is common in direct analysis; compare to is common in likeness or analogy. Contemporary usage overlaps, so do not treat this tendency as a strict rule.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the content and recipient in one complaint:


Residents complained ___ persistent construction noise ___ the city council.
column3:
Residents complained about persistent construction noise to the city council.


Use complain about + problem for the content and complain to + person/authority for the recipient.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the request and inquiry:


1. The tenant asked ___ a written receipt.
2. The tenant asked ___ the building's fire-safety record.
column3:
1. The tenant asked for a written receipt.
2. The tenant asked about the building's fire-safety record.


Use ask for + requested thing and ask about + inquiry topic.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the matched demand in two forms:


1. The auditor insisted ___ immediate disclosure.
2. The auditor insisted ___ disclosing the conflict immediately.
column3:
1. The auditor insisted on immediate disclosure.
2. The auditor insisted on disclosing the conflict immediately.


Use insist on + noun/V-ing. Do not use insist to disclose.


Also OK in formal use: insist upon immediate disclosure / insist upon disclosing the conflict.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the judgment and authorization statements with approve:


1. Many residents do not ___ converting the park into a parking lot.
2. The council did not ___ the conversion plan.
column3:
1. Many residents do not approve of converting the park into a parking lot.
2. The council did not approve the conversion plan.


Approve of + action/person means consider acceptable. Transitive approve + proposal means officially authorize it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the AmE school pattern with the safest form for careful general writing:


She ___ the University of Michigan in 2024.
column3:
She graduated from the University of Michigan in 2024.


Graduate from + institution is the most widely accepted form.


Also heard in AmE, especially with high school/college: She graduated college in 2024. Some readers object to this transitive form, so use from in careful general writing.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the service statement with the required form of subscribe:


More than 50,000 readers ___ the journal's digital edition.
column3:
More than 50,000 readers subscribe to the journal's digital edition.


Use subscribe to + service/publication for paying or signing up to receive it.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the participation statement with the required form of withdraw:


The company ___ the negotiations after the confidentiality agreement was breached.
column3:
The company withdrew from the negotiations after the confidentiality agreement was breached.


Use withdraw from + activity/negotiation for formally ending participation.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the financial transaction with the required form of withdraw:


I need to ___ $300 ___ my savings account.
column3:
I need to withdraw $300 from my savings account.


Use withdraw + money + from + account: the amount is the direct object, and the account is introduced by from.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete both statements with the required form of care:


1. Trained volunteers ___ older adults who live alone.
2. Trained volunteers deeply ___ the dignity of the people they serve.
column3:
1. Trained volunteers care for older adults who live alone.
2. Trained volunteers deeply care about the dignity of the people they serve.


Care for + dependent means look after someone. Care about + issue/person means consider that person or matter important.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the event and intended-action statements:


1. The region is preparing ___ a prolonged drought.
2. The region is preparing ___ impose water restrictions.
column3:
1. The region is preparing for a prolonged drought.
2. The region is preparing to impose water restrictions.


Use prepare for + event/thing and prepare to + verb for an intended action.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the expected arrival and delayed action:


1. We waited ___ the laboratory results.
2. We waited ___ notify the participants until the results arrived.
column3:
1. We waited for the laboratory results.
2. We waited to notify the participants until the results arrived.


Use wait for + person/thing for what is expected and wait to + verb for an action delayed until later.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the self-action and other-person action:


1. I want ___ review the evidence myself.
2. I want the committee ___ review the evidence.
column3:
1. I want to review the evidence myself.
2. I want the committee to review the evidence.


Use want + to-infinitive for the subject's action and want + person + to-infinitive for another person's action.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete sentence 1. Then answer: which frame can state a decision with a separately expressed subject—the to-infinitive in 1 or the finite clause in 2?


1. The board decided ___ postpone the vote.
2. The board decided (that) the vote should be postponed.
column3:
1. The board decided to postpone the vote.
2. The board decided (that) the vote should be postponed.


Use decide + to-infinitive for an action by the deciding subject. Use decide (that) + finite clause when the clause states the decision and may have a different subject. That may be omitted. Do not use decide the chair to postpone.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete both accepted planning frames:


1. The agency plans ___ expand the pilot next year.
2. The agency plans ___ expanding the pilot next year.
column3:
1. The agency plans to expand the pilot next year.
2. The agency plans on expanding the pilot next year.


Neutral plan + to-infinitive states an intended action. Plan on + V-ing is also common, often with a slightly more conversational tone.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete sentence 1. Then answer: which frame can name a different subject—the to-infinitive in 1 or the finite clause in 2?


1. I hope ___ present the findings in May.
2. I hope (that) Maya can present the findings in May.
column3:
1. I hope to present the findings in May.
2. I hope (that) Maya can present the findings in May.


Use hope + to-infinitive when the subject of hope will act. Use hope (that) + finite clause for another subject. That may be omitted; do not use hope Maya to present.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete sentence 1. Then answer: which frame reports promised content without making the promiser the understood actor—the to-infinitive in 1 or the finite clause in 2?


1. The contractor promised ___ repair the damage.
2. The contractor promised (that) the damage would be repaired by Friday.
column3:
1. The contractor promised to repair the damage.
2. The contractor promised (that) the damage would be repaired by Friday.


Use promise + to-infinitive for the promiser's commitment to act. Use promise (that) + finite clause to report promised content. That may be omitted.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the refusal with the required form of refuse:


The supplier refused ___ disclose its testing methods.
column3:
The supplier refused to disclose its testing methods.


Use refuse + to-infinitive, not refuse disclosing.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the difficult success and attempted action:


1. Engineers managed ___ restore the service before dawn.
2. Engineers tried ___ restore the service before dawn.
column3:
1. Engineers managed to restore the service before dawn.
2. Engineers tried to restore the service before dawn.


Manage + to-infinitive means succeed in a difficult action. Try + to-infinitive states an attempt and does not guarantee success.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the financial-capacity statement with the required form of afford:


The clinic cannot afford ___ replace the scanner this year.
column3:
The clinic cannot afford to replace the scanner this year.


Use afford + to-infinitive for having enough money, time, or capacity to act. Do not use afford replacing.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the matched preference statements:


1. I enjoy ___ complex datasets. (an activity)
2. I would like ___ complex datasets. (a desired action)
column3:
1. I enjoy analyzing complex datasets.
2. I would like to analyze complex datasets.


Use enjoy + V-ing for an activity found pleasant. Do not use enjoy to analyze.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the prevention and intention statements:
