1. The revised form avoids ___ unnecessary personal data.
2. The revised form aims ___ reduce unnecessary data collection.
column3:
1. The revised form avoids collecting unnecessary personal data.
2. The revised form aims to reduce unnecessary data collection.


Use avoid + V-ing for an action not done. Do not use avoid to collect.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the general suggestion with the required form of suggest:


The consultant suggested ___ the pilot for six months. (use extend)
column3:
The consultant suggested extending the pilot for six months.


Use suggest + V-ing for a general activity, not suggest to extend.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the option under consideration and the final intention:


1. The university is considering ___ evening classes.
2. The university intends ___ offer evening classes.
column3:
1. The university is considering offering evening classes.
2. The university intends to offer evening classes.


Use consider + V-ing for thinking about a possible action. Do not use consider to offer.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the continuing action and maintained state:


1. The sensor keeps ___ false alarms. (use trigger)
2. The backup battery keeps the sensor ___ during outages. (use operational)
column3:
1. The sensor keeps triggering false alarms.
2. The backup battery keeps the sensor operational during outages.


Use keep + V-ing for a continuing action and keep + object + adjective for maintaining a state.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the lost opportunity and forgotten duty:


1. Because her train was delayed, Lena missed ___ the opening lecture. (use hear)
2. Lena forgot ___ register for the afternoon workshop.
column3:
1. Because her train was delayed, Lena missed hearing the opening lecture.
2. Lena forgot to register for the afternoon workshop.


Use miss + V-ing for failing to experience an activity. Do not use miss to attend.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the finished activity and subsequent action:


1. The team finished ___ the survey data. (use analyze)
2. The team then proceeded ___ draft the report.
column3:
1. The team finished analyzing the survey data.
2. The team then proceeded to draft the report.


Use finish + V-ing for completing an activity. Do not use finish to analyze.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the repeated activity and its purpose:


1. Students practiced ___ the policy in plain language. (use explain)
2. They did this ___ communicate more clearly with the public.
column3:
1. Students practiced explaining the policy in plain language.
2. They did this to communicate more clearly with the public.


Use AmE practice + V-ing for an activity repeated to improve it. Do not use practice to explain.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the future duty and past memory:


1. Remember ___ lock the archive before you leave.
2. I remember ___ the archive before I left. (use lock)
column3:
1. Remember to lock the archive before you leave.
2. I remember locking the archive before I left.


Remember to do means not forget a duty. Remember doing means have a memory of a past action.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the formal announcement and past remorse:


1. We regret ___ inform you that the fellowship has been canceled.
2. The agency regrets ___ the warning signs. (use ignore)
column3:
1. We regret to inform you that the fellowship has been canceled.
2. The agency regrets ignoring the warning signs.


Formal regret to do introduces unwelcome news. Regret doing expresses remorse about a past action.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the difficult attempt and experimental solution:


1. Technicians tried ___ restore the corrupted database, but the backup was unusable.
2. If the screen freezes, try ___ the application. (use restart)
column3:
1. Technicians tried to restore the corrupted database, but the backup was unusable.
2. If the screen freezes, try restarting the application.


Try to do means attempt an action. Try doing means test a possible solution.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the purpose pause and ended activity:


1. During the drive, we stopped ___ check the tire pressure.
2. After the warning, the factory stopped ___ untreated wastewater. (use release)
column3:
1. During the drive, we stopped to check the tire pressure.
2. After the warning, the factory stopped releasing untreated wastewater.


Stop to do means pause another activity in order to act. Stop doing means cease that activity.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the next action and continued action:


1. After summarizing the evidence, the speaker went on ___ discuss policy options.
2. Despite several interruptions, the speaker went on ___ the evidence. (use summarize)
column3:
1. After summarizing the evidence, the speaker went on to discuss policy options.
2. Despite several interruptions, the speaker went on summarizing the evidence.


Go on to do introduces a next action. Go on doing means continue the same action.


Also natural and more transparent for sentence 2: The speaker continued summarizing the evidence.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the intention and necessary consequence:


1. I meant ___ send the revised figures yesterday.
2. Meeting the deadline will mean ___ through the weekend. (use work)
column3:
1. I meant to send the revised figures yesterday.
2. Meeting the deadline will mean working through the weekend.


Mean to do means intend. Mean doing means involve or have as a consequence.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the requested action and requested thing:


1. The editor asked the author ___ clarify the final paragraph.
2. The editor asked the author ___ a revised conclusion.
column3:
1. The editor asked the author to clarify the final paragraph.
2. The editor asked the author for a revised conclusion.


Use ask + person + to-infinitive for a requested action and ask + person + for + thing for a requested object.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the instruction and reported wording:


1. The supervisor told the interns ___ save a backup copy.
2. The supervisor said ___ the interns, “Save a backup copy.”
column3:
1. The supervisor told the interns to save a backup copy.
2. The supervisor said to the interns, “Save a backup copy.”


Use tell + person + to-infinitive. With say, introduce a listener with to; do not use tell to the interns.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the person-specific and general advice:


1. The physician advised Lena ___ reduce her sodium intake.
2. The guidance advises ___ sodium intake gradually. (use reduce)
column3:
1. The physician advised Lena to reduce her sodium intake.
2. The guidance advises reducing sodium intake gradually.


Use advise + person + to-infinitive for person-specific advice and advise + V-ing for general advice.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the permission with and without a named actor:


1. The policy allows employees ___ work remotely twice a week.
2. The policy allows ___ remotely twice a week. (use work)
column3:
1. The policy allows employees to work remotely twice a week.
2. The policy allows working remotely twice a week.


Use allow + person + to-infinitive when the actor is named and allow + V-ing for an activity generally. Do not use allow employees work.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the prediction with the required form of expect:


Economists expect inflation ___ fall gradually over the next year.
column3:
Economists expect inflation to fall gradually over the next year.


Use expect + person/thing + to-infinitive for a belief about what that person or thing will do. It is a prediction, not a request.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete both accepted persuasion frames:


1. The evidence persuaded the board ___ reopen the investigation.
2. The evidence persuaded the board ___ reopening the investigation.
column3:
1. The evidence persuaded the board to reopen the investigation.
2. The evidence persuaded the board into reopening the investigation.


Use persuade + person + to-infinitive. Also accepted: persuade + person + into + V-ing, often emphasizing the process or pressure.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the causative and ordinary request:


1. The outage made employees ___ the building.
2. The safety officer asked employees ___ leave the building.
column3:
1. The outage made employees leave the building.
2. The safety officer asked employees to leave the building.


Active causative make + person + bare infinitive has no to. Ask + person takes a to-infinitive.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the matched active and passive causatives:


1. The manager made the interns ___ the entire report.
2. The interns were made ___ the entire report.
column3:
1. The manager made the interns rewrite the entire report.
2. The interns were made to rewrite the entire report.


Active make + person + bare infinitive omits to. Its passive counterpart uses be made + to-infinitive.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the permission patterns:


1. The moderator let each participant ___ one final question.
2. The moderator allowed each participant ___ one final question.
column3:
1. The moderator let each participant ask one final question.
2. The moderator allowed each participant to ask one final question.


Use let + person + bare infinitive, with no to. Allow + person takes a to-infinitive.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Read the two completed AmE sentences. Are both complement forms standard?


1. The new checklist helps inspectors identify hidden hazards.
2. The new checklist helps inspectors to identify hidden hazards.
column3:
Yes. Both are standard:


1. The new checklist helps inspectors identify hidden hazards.
2. The new checklist helps inspectors to identify hidden hazards.


Use help + person + bare infinitive or help + person + to-infinitive. Neither form is an error.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the whole event and action in progress:


1. From the control room, we saw the technician ___ the valve and leave. (use close)
2. When the alarm sounded, we saw the technician ___ the valve. (use close)
column3:
1. From the control room, we saw the technician close the valve and leave.
2. When the alarm sounded, we saw the technician closing the valve.


See + person + bare infinitive presents a complete event. See + person + V-ing presents an action in progress.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the whole sound event and sound in progress:


1. I heard the alarm ___ three times and then stop. (use ring)
2. As I entered the building, I heard the alarm ___. (use ring)
column3:
1. I heard the alarm ring three times and then stop.
2. As I entered the building, I heard the alarm ringing.


Hear + object + bare infinitive presents a complete event. Hear + object + V-ing presents an activity in progress.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the resulting state and caused action:


1. The unclear instructions made the application process ___. (use confusing)
2. The unclear instructions made applicants ___ additional help. (use seek)
column3:
1. The unclear instructions made the application process confusing.
2. The unclear instructions made applicants seek additional help.


Use make + object + adjective for a resulting state and make + object + bare infinitive for a caused action.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete sentence 1. Then identify which numbered sentence uses find + object + adjective and which uses find (that) + finite clause:


1. Most participants found the online portal ___. (use confusing)
2. Most participants found (that) the online portal was difficult to navigate.
column3:
1. Most participants found the online portal confusing.
2. Most participants found (that) the online portal was difficult to navigate.


Use find + object + adjective to evaluate the object directly. Use find (that) + finite clause to report a conclusion. That may be omitted.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the arranged service and persuaded person:


1. We need to get the ventilation system ___ before winter. (use inspect)
2. We need to get the contractor ___ the ventilation system before winter. (use inspect)
column3:
1. We need to get the ventilation system inspected before winter.
2. We need to get the contractor to inspect the ventilation system before winter.


Use get + object + past participle to arrange for work to be done. Use get + person + to-infinitive when naming the person persuaded or caused to act.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Express the same transfer in both recipient orders:


1. The foundation gave the research team a two-year grant.
2. The foundation gave ___ ___.
column3:
1. The foundation gave the research team a two-year grant.
2. The foundation gave a two-year grant to the research team.


Use give + person + thing or give + thing + to + person.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Express the same transfer in both recipient orders:


1. The laboratory sent each participant a copy of the results.
2. The laboratory sent ___ ___.
column3:
1. The laboratory sent each participant a copy of the results.
2. The laboratory sent a copy of the results to each participant.


Use send + person + thing or send + thing + to + person.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Express the same beneficiary relationship in both orders:


1. The department bought the interns new safety equipment.
2. The department bought ___ ___.
column3:
1. The department bought the interns new safety equipment.
2. The department bought new safety equipment for the interns.


Use buy + person + thing or buy + thing + for + person. The beneficiary form uses for, not to.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the same report with say and tell:


1. The director ___ that the schedule would change.
2. The director ___ the staff that the schedule would change.
column3:
1. The director said (that) the schedule would change.
2. The director told the staff (that) the schedule would change.


Use say + (that-)clause. Use tell + person + (that-)clause; tell normally requires the listener, while say the staff is incorrect. That is often omitted in both frames.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the information request with the required forms of ask:


At the briefing, Maya ___ the engineer ___ the backup system had failed.
column3:
At the briefing, Maya asked the engineer why the backup system had failed.


Use ask + person + wh-clause to request information. A noun question is also possible: Maya asked the engineer a difficult question.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the method report with the required form of explain:


The guide explains ___ residents can test their drinking water.
column3:
The guide explains how residents can test their drinking water.


Use explain + wh-clause to give a reason, method, or other requested detail.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the general recommendation and AmE formal proposal:


1. The panel recommends ___ the bridge before winter. (use repair)
2. The panel recommends that the city ___ the bridge before winter.
column3:
1. The panel recommends repairing the bridge before winter.
2. The panel recommends that the city repair the bridge before winter.


Use recommend + V-ing for an activity generally. In formal AmE, use recommend that + subject + base verb. Do not use recommend the city to repair.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the AmE proposal and a person-directed request:


1. The auditor suggested that the agency ___ the contract. (use review)
2. The auditor advised the agency ___ the contract. (use review)
column3:
1. The auditor suggested that the agency review the contract.
2. The auditor advised the agency to review the contract.


Formal AmE uses suggest (that) + subject + base verb; that may be omitted. Suggest has no person + to-infinitive frame; use advise + person + to-infinitive when appropriate.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
The monitor is off; please turn it on before the presentation.
column3:
Correct as written.


The monitor is off; please turn it on before the presentation.


With separable turn on, a pronoun object goes between the verb and particle: turn it on, not turn on it. A noun may follow either order: turn on the monitor / turn the monitor on.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
The courier will pick up it from reception at noon.
column3:
The courier will pick it up from reception at noon.


With separable pick up, a pronoun object goes between the verb and particle. A noun allows both orders: pick up the package / pick the package up.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
Investigators looked the missing inspection report for all morning.
column3:
Investigators looked for the missing inspection report all morning.


Look for + object is a nonseparable verb-plus-preposition pattern. Do not place the object between look and for.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
The research team looks forward to present its findings at the conference.
column3:
The research team looks forward to presenting its findings at the conference.


In look forward to, to is a preposition, so a following action takes V-ing.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete the past habit and present familiarity:


1. Before relocating, Elena used to ___ to the office five days a week. (use commute)
2. She is now used to ___ with colleagues across several time zones. (use collaborate)
column3:
1. Before relocating, Elena used to commute to the office five days a week.
2. She is now used to collaborating with colleagues across several time zones.


Used to + base verb describes a past habit or state. Be/get used to + noun/V-ing means be or become accustomed to something; here to is a preposition.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Complete each diagnostic conclusion with out or in.


1. The scan showed no evidence of a fracture, so the doctor ruled it ___.
2. A highly specific test confirmed the infection, so the doctor ruled it ___.
column3:
1. The doctor ruled it out.
2. The doctor ruled it in.


Rule out means eliminate something as a possibility. Rule in means establish or include something as a likely diagnosis or explanation; it is much less common and is used especially in medical and technical contexts.


Both are separable: rule the condition out/in and rule it out/in, not rule out/in it.


Additional patterns:


- rule out + noun: We can't rule out a delay.
- rule out + V-ing: We can't rule out postponing the launch.
- rule someone out of + event/role: Her injury ruled her out of the final.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::02 Verb Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:
I gonna send the revised proposal tonight.
column3:
I'm gonna send the revised proposal tonight.


Casual gonna is the spoken form of going to, but it still requires the
correct form of be: I'm gonna, you're gonna, or she's gonna.
Use gonna + base verb. Prefer going to in formal and most professional
writing.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: interested ___ + topic or activity
column3:
Use interested in + noun/V-ing for something a person wants to learn about
or take part in.


- Several graduates are interested in working in renewable energy.
- I became interested in urban planning after attending a public hearing.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the matched pair.


1. Maya is interested ___ the ethics of artificial intelligence.
(Maya feels interest)
2. The ethical debate is interesting ___ Maya. (the debate causes Maya's
interest)
column3:
1. Maya is interested in the ethics of artificial intelligence.
2. The ethical debate is interesting to Maya.


Use person + be interested in + topic for the experiencer's feeling. Use
thing + be interesting to + person for the thing that causes the interest.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the two connections after concerned.


1. Residents are concerned ___ whether the new dam can withstand a major
earthquake. (worried)
2. The engineering review is concerned ___ the dam's structural
integrity. (deals with that subject)
column3:
1. Residents are **concerned about whether the new dam can withstand a major
earthquake**.
2. The engineering review is **concerned with the dam's structural
integrity**.


Use concerned about + issue/question for worry. Use
concerned with + subject for involvement or subject matter.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Give both normal forms for concern about a person's welfare.


After three days without contact, her colleagues were deeply concerned
___ her.
column3:
After three days without contact, her colleagues were deeply **concerned
about/for her**.


Both forms are normal for someone's welfare. Concerned for can foreground
sympathetic concern for the person; concerned about is fully natural too.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: aware ___ + fact, risk, or situation
column3:
Use aware of + noun when someone knows that a fact, risk, or situation
exists.


- Most consumers are aware of the privacy risks associated with facial
recognition.
- The committee was aware of a significant gap in the evidence.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: conscious ___ + fact, effect, or personal state
column3:
Use conscious of + noun for awareness of a fact, an effect, or one's own
state.


- Good interviewers remain conscious of their own assumptions.
- The architect was conscious of the building's historical significance.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Give the neutral topic default and the accepted field-oriented alternatives:


knowledgeable ___ + topic or field
column3:
Use knowledgeable about + topic as the neutral general-purpose form.
Knowledgeable in + field/area is natural for expertise within a field,
and knowledgeable of + topic is also accepted.


- The adviser is highly knowledgeable about international tax law.
- The new coordinator is **knowledgeable in several areas of environmental
policy**.


Also OK: knowledgeable of the area's flood history.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the noun and embedded-question frames. Give both normal answers
where the prompt asks for two.


1. The board is not yet certain ___ the long-term cost of the proposal.
(two normal answers)
2. Are you certain ___ which data set the report used? (neutral default)
column3:
1. The board is not yet certain about/of the long-term cost of the
proposal.
2. Are you certain about which data set the report used?


Certain about works naturally before a noun or embedded question.
Certain of overlaps strongly before a noun. Certain that + clause
states a complete proposition.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the noun and embedded-question frames. Give both normal answers
where the prompt asks for two.


1. I am not sure ___ the revised deadline. (two normal answers)
2. The researchers were sure ___ how the samples should be stored.
(neutral default)
column3:
1. I am not sure about/of the revised deadline.
2. The researchers were sure about how the samples should be stored.


Sure about works naturally before a noun or embedded question.
Sure of overlaps strongly before a noun. Sure that + clause introduces
a complete proposition.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the duty and accountability statements.


1. The contractor is responsible ___ inspecting the bridge every six
months. (duty)
2. The contractor is responsible ___ the regional transport authority.
(answerable to an authority)
column3:
1. The contractor is **responsible for inspecting the bridge every six
months**.
2. The contractor is responsible to the regional transport authority.


Use responsible for + duty/outcome to name what someone must do or caused.
Use responsible to + authority/group to name whom they answer to.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete both ability structures.


1. Modern language models are capable ___ producing fluent summaries.
2. Skilled editors are able ___ detect subtle inconsistencies.
column3:
1. Modern language models are capable of producing fluent summaries.
2. Skilled editors are able to detect subtle inconsistencies.


Use capable of + noun/V-ing, not capable to do. Use
able to + base verb for the corresponding infinitive pattern.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:


The outdated system is incapable to process encrypted files.
column3:
The outdated system is incapable of processing encrypted files.


Use incapable of + noun/V-ing, not incapable to + verb.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the skill and handling statements.


1. Priya is particularly good ___ explaining technical risks to clients.
2. She is also good ___ anxious clients. (she handles relationships well)
column3:
1. Priya is particularly good at explaining technical risks to clients.
2. She is also good with anxious clients.


Use good at + activity for skill in doing something. Use
good with + people/things for handling or relating to them well.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: bad ___ + activity
column3:
Use bad at + noun/V-ing for a skill or activity someone does poorly.


- I am bad at estimating how long complex tasks will take.
- The previous administration was bad at communicating policy changes.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Choose in or at as the conventional default; use each once.


1. Applicants must be proficient ___ written and spoken Spanish.
(language/field)
2. The mediator is proficient ___ resolving complex workplace disputes.
(specific task)
column3:
1. Applicants must be proficient in written and spoken Spanish.
2. The mediator is proficient at resolving complex workplace disputes.


Use proficient in + field/language as the conventional field-oriented
frame. Use proficient at + task/activity for performance of a specific
task.


Also OK: The prepositions can overlap with activities; this card teaches
the useful default preference, not an absolute boundary.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete this natural description:


The mediator is skilled ___ resolving disputes between departments.
column3:
The mediator is skilled at resolving disputes between departments.


Use skilled at + activity to emphasize performance of a particular
activity.


- The surgeon is skilled at performing minimally invasive procedures.
- Our analysts are skilled at identifying patterns in incomplete data.


Also OK: skilled in resolving disputes is natural; skilled in often
frames the activity as an area of expertise.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: relevant ___ + topic, decision, problem, or situation
column3:
Use relevant to + matter when information or a consideration directly
bears on the issue being discussed.


- The panel excluded evidence that was not relevant to the investigation.
- Cost is highly **relevant to the decision about whether to expand the
service**.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: applicable ___ + case, group, or situation
column3:
Use applicable to + case/group/situation when a rule, method, or
requirement can be used there.


- The revised safety standard is applicable to all commercial laboratories.
- This exemption is not applicable to employees hired after January 1.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: suitable ___ + purpose, person, or activity
column3:
Use suitable for + noun/V-ing when something is right for an intended
purpose, person, or activity.


- The software is suitable for managing small research projects.
- This documentary is suitable for a general audience.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: appropriate ___ + intended audience or use
column3:
Use appropriate for + noun/V-ing when something fits an intended audience
or use.


- The language in the leaflet is appropriate for younger readers.
- This method is not appropriate for measuring very small changes.


Also OK in a different matching frame: **appropriate to the
circumstances / appropriate to the crime**.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the access and purpose statements.


1. Free legal advice is available ___ low-income residents. (who can access
it)
2. Additional funding is available ___ emergency repairs. (intended use)
column3:
1. Free legal advice is available to low-income residents.
2. Additional funding is available for emergency repairs.


Use available to + person/group for access. Use
available for + use/purpose for what something can be used for.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete with the neutral default, then name the common alternative:


beneficial ___ + recipient
column3:
Use beneficial to + recipient for something that has a helpful effect on
that person, system, or outcome.


- Regular physical activity is **beneficial to both mental and physical
health**.
- Greater transparency would be beneficial to the entire organization.


Also OK: beneficial for is common in the same broad benefit contexts;
do not force a categorical meaning contrast.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete with the neutral default, then name the common alternative:


harmful ___ + affected person, system, or environment
column3:
Use harmful to + recipient for something that damages or adversely affects
that person, system, or environment.


- Prolonged noise exposure can be harmful to children's development.
- The invasive species is harmful to native ecosystems.


Also OK: harmful for is common, especially with affected groups.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the purpose and beneficiary statements.


1. Satellite images are useful ___ monitoring illegal logging. (purpose)
2. The weekly summary is useful ___ regional managers. (beneficiary)
column3:
1. Satellite images are useful for monitoring illegal logging.
2. The weekly summary is useful to regional managers.


Use useful for + purpose/activity for what something helps accomplish.
Use useful to + person/group for whom it helps.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: similar ___ + comparison item
column3:
Use similar to + noun when two things share important features.


- The proposed tax credit is similar to a program introduced in Canada.
- The symptoms are similar to those of seasonal influenza.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
different ___ + noun or comparison clause (give the neutral default and
accepted AmE alternative)
column3:
Use different from + comparison as the neutral general-purpose form.


- The final agreement was different from the draft circulated in May.
- Working remotely is different from sharing an office with your team.


Also OK in AmE: different than is accepted with nouns and clauses:
The outcome was different than we had expected. Different from also
works before a clause.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Give both accepted prepositions:


comparable ___ + item used as a standard
column3:
Use comparable to/with + item when two things are similar enough for a
meaningful comparison. Both are standard; to is a natural default in
these examples.


- The new battery's performance is **comparable to that of the leading
model**.
- Housing costs in the two regional capitals are broadly **comparable to each
other**.


Also OK: comparable with in both examples.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: compatible ___ + system, requirement, or person
column3:
Use compatible with + noun when two systems, requirements, or people can
work or exist together.


- The application is **compatible with older versions of the operating
system**.
- The proposed schedule is not compatible with current staffing levels.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: associated ___ + thing, condition, or idea
column3:
Use associated with + noun for a connection established by evidence,
experience, or common belief.


- Chronic sleep deprivation is **associated with a higher risk of
depression**.
- The neighborhood was once associated with heavy industry.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: based ___ + evidence, source, or principle
column3:
Use based on + evidence/source/principle for the foundation of a claim,
decision, or design.


- The recommendation is based on evidence from three clinical trials.
- Eligibility is based on household income and residency status.


Also OK in informal AmE: based off and based off of occur
frequently. Prefer based on in neutral and formal writing.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the location and evidence statements.


1. The humanitarian organization is based ___ Nairobi. (main location)
2. Its relief strategy is based ___ local assessments. (foundation)
column3:
1. The humanitarian organization is based in Nairobi.
2. Its relief strategy is based on local assessments.


Use based in + place for an organization's or person's main location. Use
based on + evidence/source for a foundation.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the dependency frame.


Whether the project proceeds is dependent ___ final regulatory approval.
column3:
Whether the project proceeds is dependent on final regulatory approval.


Use dependent on + factor/question when an outcome needs or is determined
by something.


- The project schedule is dependent on winter weather conditions.
- Final approval is **dependent upon the completion of an environmental
review**.


Also OK: dependent upon is a more formal variant.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Choose of or from as the natural default in these contexts; use each
once.


1. The inquiry must remain independent ___ political pressure.
(freedom from influence)
2. In 2019, the newspaper became institutionally independent ___ its
former owner. (separation)
column3:
1. The inquiry must remain independent of political pressure.
2. In 2019, the newspaper became institutionally **independent from its
former owner**.


Use independent of + influence/resource as the neutral default for
nondependence. Independent from is accepted and especially natural when
foregrounding separation or an institutional relationship.


Also OK for sentence 2: independent of its former owner.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Choose with or by; use each once.


1. Most patients were satisfied ___ the quality of follow-up care.
(evaluated service)
2. Demand for evening appointments was partly satisfied ___ extending
clinic hours. (means that met the demand)
column3:
1. Most patients were satisfied with the quality of follow-up care.
2. Demand for evening appointments was partly **satisfied by extending
clinic hours**.


Use satisfied with + evaluated object/result when it meets someone's
expectations. Use passive satisfied by + cause/means for what fulfills a
need or requirement.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: dissatisfied ___ + result, service, or decision
column3:
Use dissatisfied with + evaluated thing when it fails to meet someone's
expectations.


- Residents were dissatisfied with the council's response to the flooding.
- Several employees remain dissatisfied with the revised promotion policy.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the evaluation and reaction frames after pleased.


1. The auditors were pleased ___ the quality of the final report.
(evaluation)
2. Staff were pleased ___ the announcement of additional leave.
(reaction to news)
column3:
1. The auditors were pleased with the quality of the final report.
2. Staff were pleased about the announcement of additional leave.


Use pleased with + evaluated object/result for a positive judgment. Use
pleased about + event/news for a positive reaction. The two frames can
overlap when an event is also being evaluated.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the evaluation and cause frames. Give both normal answers where the
prompt asks for two.


1. Voters were disappointed ___ the government's response to the housing
crisis. (evaluated response; two normal answers)
2. Residents were disappointed ___ the sudden cancellation of the public
hearing. (event causing the reaction; foreground the cause)
column3:
1. Voters were **disappointed with/in the government's response to the
housing crisis**.
2. Residents were **disappointed by the sudden cancellation of the public
hearing**.


Use disappointed with/in + evaluated person, institution, or result when
expectations were not met. Use disappointed by + cause/event when
foregrounding what produced the reaction.


Also OK for sentence 2: disappointed about/at the sudden cancellation
are natural reaction frames.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete this natural reaction:


The medical team was amazed ___ how quickly the patient recovered.
column3:
The medical team was amazed at how quickly the patient recovered.


Use amazed at/by + event or fact for a very strong reaction of surprise.


- Economists were amazed at the speed of the recovery.
- We were amazed by the generosity of local volunteers.


Also OK: amazed by how quickly the patient recovered. Both at and
by are accepted; by often foregrounds the cause of the reaction.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete this natural reaction:


The inspectors were surprised ___ how little damage the building had
sustained.
column3:
The inspectors were **surprised at how little damage the building had
sustained**.


Use surprised at/by + event or fact for an unexpected reaction.


- Researchers were surprised at the scale of public support.
- I was surprised by the sudden change in tone.


Also OK: surprised by how little damage the building had sustained.
Both at and by are accepted; by more clearly foregrounds what
caused the surprise.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete this natural reaction:


Residents were shocked ___ the extent of the contamination.
column3:
Residents were shocked by the extent of the contamination.


Use shocked by/at + event or fact for a strong reaction of distress or
surprise.


- Staff were shocked by the abrupt closure of the factory.
- The committee was shocked at the number of unreported incidents.


Also OK: shocked at the extent of the contamination. Both by and
at are accepted; by often foregrounds the immediate cause.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Give the neutral default and accepted alternatives:


angry ___ + issue, event, or action
column3:
Use angry about + noun/V-ing for the issue, event, or action causing
anger.


- Residents are angry about the proposed closure of the local clinic.
- She was angry about being excluded from the negotiations.


Also OK: angry at/over + issue or action can be natural.
Use angry with/at + person when directing the anger toward someone.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete this natural directed reaction:


The client was angry ___ the consultant for withholding crucial information.
column3:
The client was **angry with the consultant for withholding crucial
information**.


Use angry with/at + person when the anger is directed toward that person.


- Several parents were angry with the school board.
- The union was **angry at management for changing the schedule without
notice**.


Also OK: angry at the consultant. Both with and at are accepted
in AmE. Use angry about + issue/action to name the cause rather than the
target.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete this natural directed reaction:


I was annoyed ___ the supplier for repeatedly missing delivery dates.
column3:
I was annoyed with the supplier for repeatedly missing delivery dates.


Use annoyed with/at + person when irritation is directed toward that
person.


- Commuters were annoyed with the operator over the lack of information.
- She was annoyed at her colleague for interrupting the presentation.


Also OK: annoyed at the supplier. Both with and at are accepted
for a person in AmE.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the cause and person-target frames after annoyed. Give all normal
answers for each sentence.


1. Employees were annoyed ___ the last-minute change. (cause)
2. Employees were annoyed ___ the manager. (person targeted)
column3:
1. Employees were annoyed by/at the last-minute change.
2. Employees were annoyed with/at the manager.


Use annoyed by/at + cause for what produced the irritation. Use
annoyed with/at + person for its target.


Also OK: annoyed about/over the last-minute change are accepted issue
frames; the prepositions overlap, so do not force a categorical boundary.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: worried ___ + problem, future event, or embedded question
column3:
Use worried about + noun/wh-clause for anxiety about a problem, possible
event, or unresolved question.


- Many graduates are worried about finding stable employment.
- Public-health officials are **worried about whether vaccination rates will
recover**.


Also OK: worried over + issue occurs, especially when emphasizing an
ongoing concern.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: nervous ___ + event or activity
column3:
Use nervous about + noun/V-ing for anxiety regarding an event, outcome, or
activity.


- She felt nervous about presenting her findings to the board.
- Investors are nervous about the possibility of another recession.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the fear of an activity and the fear that prevents an action.


1. Some patients are afraid ___ undergoing the procedure. (the activity
itself is feared)
2. Others are afraid ___ ask questions. (fear makes them unwilling to act)
column3:
1. Some patients are afraid of undergoing the procedure.
2. Others are afraid to ask questions.


Use afraid of + noun/V-ing for the thing or activity feared. Use
afraid to + base verb when fear prevents or discourages an action.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the general fear and immediate-cause frames after frightened.


1. The child is frightened ___ unfamiliar dogs. (general object of fear)
2. The child was frightened ___ a sudden explosion. (event that caused
the reaction)
column3:
1. The child is frightened of unfamiliar dogs.
2. The child was frightened by a sudden explosion.


Use frightened of + noun/V-ing for a general object or activity feared.
Use frightened by + immediate cause for what produced the reaction. Some
real contexts overlap, so rely on the printed meanings here.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the enthusiasm for an idea and the eagerness to act.


1. The mayor is keen ___ expanding the bicycle network. (enthusiastic about
the idea)
2. She is keen ___ begin construction next year. (eager to act)
column3:
1. The mayor is keen on expanding the bicycle network.
2. She is keen to begin construction next year.


Use keen on + noun/V-ing for enthusiasm about an activity or idea. Use
keen to + base verb for eagerness to perform an action.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: fond ___ + person, place, or activity
column3:
Use fond of + noun/V-ing for warm liking or affection.


- My grandfather is fond of telling stories about his childhood.
- She remains deeply fond of the coastal town where she grew up.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: proud ___ + achievement or action
column3:
Use proud of + noun/V-ing for pleasure in an achievement or action.


- The community is proud of restoring the historic theater.
- She is proud of her students' progress during the semester.


Also OK in a different meaning frame: proud for + person means happy
on that person's behalf after their success.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: ashamed ___ + action or personal quality
column3:
Use ashamed of + noun/V-ing for shame about an action, behavior, or
quality.


- The company should be ashamed of concealing the safety data.
- He felt ashamed of his dismissive attitude toward junior colleagues.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the reason for gratitude and the person receiving it.


1. We are grateful ___ the volunteers' sustained support.
2. We are grateful ___ the volunteers who organized the relief effort.
column3:
1. We are grateful for the volunteers' sustained support.
2. We are grateful to the volunteers who organized the relief effort.


Use grateful for + benefit/action to name the reason for gratitude. Use
grateful to + person to name whom the gratitude is directed toward.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: famous ___ + feature, product, or achievement
column3:
Use famous for + noun/V-ing to name the feature or achievement that gives
someone or something a wide reputation.


- The region is famous for producing high-quality olive oil.
- The university is famous for its pioneering medical research.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the reason for recognition and the recognized role.


1. The city is known ___ its extensive network of public parks.
2. It is known ___ the nation's greenest capital.
column3:
1. The city is known for its extensive network of public parks.
2. It is known as the nation's greenest capital.


Use known for + feature/achievement to name why something is recognized.
Use known as + name/role/category to name its identity.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: be caused ___ + source of an event, condition, or problem
column3:
Use be caused by + noun/V-ing in a passive clause to name what produces an
event, condition, or problem.


- The service disruption was caused by a failure in the cooling system.
- Much of the delay was **caused by contractors having to verify incomplete
records**.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Choose related or relevant; use each once. Keep to.


1. The appendix contains documents ___ to the merger. (general connection)
2. Only two of those documents are ___ to the dispute before the court.
(directly bears on the matter)
column3:
1. The appendix contains documents related to the merger.
2. Only two of those documents are **relevant to the dispute before the
court**.


Related to states a connection. Relevant to means that something
directly bears on the matter being considered.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Express the same probability with the named subject and with extraposed
it.


1. The bill is likely ___ pass with bipartisan support.
2. It is likely ___ the bill will pass with bipartisan support.
column3:
1. The bill is likely to pass with bipartisan support.
2. It is likely that the bill will pass with bipartisan support.


In subject + be likely to + verb, the main-clause subject is also the
semantic subject of the infinitive. It need not be an intentional agent:
The economy is likely to recover is equally natural.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the action and event forms.


1. The emergency team is ready ___ deploy within thirty minutes. (action)
2. The emergency team is ready ___ the approaching storm. (event)
column3:
1. The emergency team is ready to deploy within thirty minutes.
2. The emergency team is ready for the approaching storm.


Use ready to + base verb for an action someone is prepared or willing to
perform. Use ready for + noun for an event, situation, or thing.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: reluctant ___ + base verb
column3:
Use reluctant to + base verb when someone is hesitant or unwilling to
perform an action.


- Some employers remain reluctant to adopt a four-day workweek.
- Witnesses may be reluctant to report misconduct without legal
protection.


Also OK in a different complement frame: reluctant about + noun/V-ing
can express hesitation about a proposal or activity.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete these high-frequency reaction chunks:


pleased ___ announce ... / pleased ___ hear ... / pleased ___ meet ...
column3:
Use pleased to announce/hear/meet + complement for a positive reaction to
performing an action or receiving information.


- We are **pleased to announce that the scholarship fund has reached its
target**.
- I was pleased to hear that your recovery is progressing well.
- The director **will be pleased to meet the community representatives this
afternoon**.


Use pleased with + noun instead to evaluate a result or object:
The director was pleased with the final report.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the known proposition and the known risk.


1. Regulators were aware ___ the company had withheld safety data.
2. Regulators were aware ___ the missing safety data.
column3:
1. Regulators were aware that the company had withheld safety data.
2. Regulators were aware of the missing safety data.


Use aware that + complete clause for a known proposition. Use
aware of + noun for a known fact, thing, or situation.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the unwanted proposition and the issue.


1. Doctors are concerned ___ antibiotic resistance is spreading rapidly.
2. Doctors are concerned ___ the rapid spread of antibiotic resistance.
column3:
1. Doctors are concerned that antibiotic resistance is spreading rapidly.
2. Doctors are concerned about the rapid spread of antibiotic resistance.


Use concerned that + complete clause to state the feared proposition. Use
concerned about + noun to name the issue.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the proposition and the matter.


1. Investigators are certain ___ the signature was forged.
2. Investigators are certain ___ the document's origin.
column3:
1. Investigators are certain that the signature was forged.
2. Investigators are certain about the document's origin.


Use certain that + complete clause for a proposition judged true. Use
certain about + noun for confidence about a matter.


Also OK: certain of the document's origin is natural; do not treat
certain of as wrong.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Choose whether or how; use each once after unsure.


1. Officials are unsure ___ the river will remain within its banks.
(uncertain outcome)
2. Many small firms are unsure ___ they can comply with the new reporting
rules. (uncertain method)
column3:
1. Officials are unsure whether the river will remain within its banks.
2. Many small firms are **unsure how they can comply with the new reporting
rules**.


Use unsure whether + clause for uncertainty about an outcome. Use
unsure how + clause for uncertainty about a method or way to proceed.


Also OK: uncertain whether/how + clause has the same core meaning.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Use easy/hard to or easy/hard for ... to while keeping the roles
clear.


1. This manual is easy ___ use. (the manual is the understood object of
use)
2. It is easy ___ new staff ___ use this manual. (new staff perform
use)
3. These instructions are hard ___ follow without a diagram. (the
instructions are the understood object of follow)
column3:
1. This manual is easy to use.
2. It is easy for new staff to use this manual.
3. These instructions are hard to follow without a diagram.


In X is easy/hard to use, X is understood as the object of the
infinitive: someone uses the manual. In
It is easy/hard for person to use X, for + person explicitly names the
performer.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Fix if wrong:


The proposal is worth to consider because it could substantially reduce
housing costs.
column3:
The proposal is worth considering because it could substantially reduce
housing costs.


Use worth + V-ing, not worth to + base verb, when an action warrants the
time or effort.


Also OK in a different AmE frame: `It is worth it to consider the
proposal.` The pronoun it is required in that construction; direct
worth to consider remains wrong.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Choose likely to or liable to as the conventional default in these
contexts; use each once.


1. Household energy demand is ___ remain high this winter.
(neutral probability)
2. Without regular maintenance, older heat pumps are ___ fail during a cold
snap. (risk)
column3:
1. Household energy demand is likely to remain high this winter.
2. Without regular maintenance, older heat pumps are **liable to fail during
a cold snap**.


Use likely to + base verb for general probability. Use
liable to + base verb when the context frames a risk, susceptibility, or
recurring tendency.


Also OK: liable to can sometimes mean simply “likely to,” so the
negative association is a strong tendency, not an absolute rule.
With a noun, liable to + noun can express susceptibility:
Low-lying neighborhoods are liable to flooding.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete the action-importance and person-evaluation frames.


1. It is important ___ every applicant ___ disclose any conflict of
interest. (the action matters)
2. It was kind ___ Lena ___ check on her elderly neighbor. (Lena's action
shows kindness)
column3:
1. It is **important for every applicant to disclose any conflict of
interest**.
2. It was kind of Lena to check on her elderly neighbor.


Use It is + adjective + for + person + to-inf when the adjective evaluates
the situation or action and for + person names its performer. Use
It is/was + adjective + of + person + to-inf when the adjective evaluates
the person's behavior or character.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2: be legally liable ___ + damages, costs, or loss
column3:
Use be legally liable for + noun when a person or organization has legal
responsibility for damages, costs, or a loss.


- A data processor may be **legally liable for losses caused by inadequate
security controls**.
- Under the settlement, the contractor is **liable for the cost of repairing
the defective bridge supports**.


This is separate from liable to + base verb, which describes likelihood,
risk, or tendency.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::03 Adjective and Participle Patterns
column2:
Complete with daily, every day, or everyday.


1. Our team holds a ___ stand-up meeting. (it happens each day)
2. Our team holds a stand-up meeting ___. (each day)
3. Clear communication is essential in ___ work. (ordinary or routine)
column3:
1. Our team holds a daily stand-up meeting.
2. Our team holds a stand-up meeting every day.
3. Clear communication is essential in everyday work.


Daily can be an adjective meaning *happening every day* or an adverb
meaning *every day*. Every day is a two-word time expression. Everyday
is an adjective meaning *ordinary or routine*, so it comes before a noun.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Complete the first two reason frames, then answer the recognition question.


1. The lack of reliable data was the main reason ___ delaying the launch.
(motive or basis)
2. The new safety evidence gives regulators a reason ___ revise the policy.
(action justified)
3. Give all three standard possibilities before the explanatory clause:
the reason ___ the clinic closed.
column3:
1. The lack of reliable data was the main reason for delaying the launch.
2. The new safety evidence gives regulators a reason to revise the policy.
3. All three are standard: the reason why the clinic closed,
the reason that the clinic closed, and
the reason the clinic closed.


Use reason for + NP/V-ing for a motive or basis and reason to + base verb
for a justified action. Before an explanatory clause, why, that, and
zero are overlapping standard choices. Reason of is not the standard frame
for any of these meanings.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: the/a cause ___ + event or condition
column3:
Use the/a cause of + event or condition for the factor that produces it.


- Researchers are investigating **the cause of the sudden decline in bee
populations**.
- Chronic sleep deprivation is a major cause of workplace accidents.


A cause produces an outcome; a reason commonly explains or motivates
an action or belief.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Complete the noun frame with the preposition that introduces the event that
produced the outcome:


The service interruption was the result ___ a failed software update.
column3:
The service interruption was the result of a failed software update.


Use result of + event/action after the noun result to name what produced
the outcome. The verb frame is different: `A failed update resulted in a
service interruption.`

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Complete the matched effect descriptions. For sentence 1, give both
accepted source connectors.


1. The study examined the effect ___ prolonged screen exposure.
(the source being evaluated)
2. The study examined the effect of prolonged screen exposure ___ sleep
quality. (the affected target)
column3:
1. The study examined the effect of/from prolonged screen exposure.
2. The study examined **the effect of prolonged screen exposure on sleep
quality**.


Use effect of + cause/source when the source is the thing being evaluated;
effect from + cause/source can more directly present causal origin. Use
effect on + target to name what is affected. The verb affect takes a
direct object: Screen exposure may affect sleep quality.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Complete the matched impact descriptions. For sentence 1, give both
accepted source connectors.


1. Economists assessed the impact ___ the new carbon tax.
(the source being evaluated)
2. Economists assessed the impact of the new carbon tax ___ small
manufacturers. (the affected target)
column3:
1. Economists assessed the impact of/from the new carbon tax.
2. Economists assessed **the impact of the new carbon tax on small
manufacturers**.


Use impact of + cause/source when the source is the thing being evaluated;
impact from + cause/source can more directly present causal origin. Use
impact on + target for the person, group, or system affected. As a verb,
impact takes a direct object: The tax may impact small manufacturers.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Match each completed frame to its conventional emphasis, then state whether
the distinction is absolute.


1. the comments' influence on the final vote
2. the chair's influence over the committee
column3:
1. Influence on tends to foreground an observed effect.
2. Influence over tends to foreground power to shape a person, body, or
decision.


These are useful tendencies, not categorical opposites. Real contexts may
support either construal.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
a solution to the housing shortage


What is the conventional neutral noun frame, and what common variant may also
occur?
column3:
Prefer solution to + problem as the conventional neutral learner default.


- Affordable childcare is not a complete solution to the labor shortage.
- The engineering team proposed **a practical solution to the drainage
problem**.


Also OK: solution for + problem occurs in contemporary AmE.
Solution for + person/purpose also commonly names the intended user or use,
as in a payment solution for small businesses.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: an approach ___ + topic or V-ing activity
column3:
Use an approach to + NP/V-ing for a method of dealing with a subject,
problem, or activity.


- The course takes an interdisciplinary approach to public health.
- The city needs **a more systematic approach to reducing traffic
congestion**.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
an answer to the housing affordability problem


What is the conventional neutral noun frame, and where can for occur?
column3:
Prefer the/an answer to + question/problem for a response or solution.


- The panel never gave a clear answer to the reporter's question.
- There is no simple answer to the housing affordability problem.


Also OK in other noun frames: an answer for someone and, in some
contexts, an answer for a problem. The verb phrase answer for + action is a
different accountability pattern.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: a response ___ + question, event, proposal, or action
column3:
Use a response to + stimulus for an answer or reaction prompted by
something.


- The ministry issued a detailed response to the audit findings.
- Emergency funding was approved in response to the severe flooding.


A response may be deliberate; reaction to often foregrounds what an
event causes someone to feel or do.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: a reaction ___ + event, statement, or action
column3:
Use a reaction to + event/action for the response caused by it.


- Public reaction to the proposed surveillance law was overwhelmingly
negative.
- Her immediate reaction to the diagnosis was one of disbelief.


Response to is broader and can describe a deliberate answer as well as a
reaction.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Enrollment rose from 8,000 to 10,000 students.


1. The university reported a 25 percent increase ___ enrollment.
(the variable that rose)
2. This was an increase ___ 2,000 students.
(the numerical size of the rise)
column3:
1. The university reported a 25 percent increase in enrollment.
2. This was an increase of 2,000 students.


Use increase in + variable to name what rose. Use
increase of + amount to name the size of the rise.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Average household water use fell from 300 to 255 gallons per day.


1. The city recorded a 15 percent decrease ___ average household water use.
(the variable that fell)
2. This was a decrease ___ 45 gallons per household per day.
(the numerical size of the fall)
column3:
1. The city recorded a 15 percent **decrease in average household water
use**.
2. This was a decrease of 45 gallons per household per day.


Use decrease in + variable to name what fell. Use
decrease of + amount to name the size of the fall.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Complete the noun frame for an alteration affecting the measured variable:


Researchers detected a statistically significant change ___ average sea
surface temperature.
column3:
Researchers detected **a statistically significant change in average sea
surface temperature**.


Use change in + variable/domain for an alteration within that variable or
domain. Do not infer a general change of + amount rule; **a change of
address or a change of leadership** commonly describes replacement, not
the size of a numerical change.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Complete with between or in.


1. The review found a substantial difference ___ the two screening methods.
(two items compared)
2. The review found a substantial difference ___ diagnostic accuracy.
(the feature that varies)
column3:
1. The review found a substantial **difference between the two screening
methods**.
2. The review found a substantial difference in diagnostic accuracy.


Use difference between + two or more items to name the items compared. Use
difference in + feature to name the area in which they vary.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: a/the need ___ + thing or person
column3:
Use a/the need for + NP for something or someone that is required.


- The pandemic highlighted the need for reliable broadband access.
- Several rural hospitals reported an urgent need for trained nurses.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: demand ___ + product, service, or resource
column3:
Use demand for + product/service/resource for the desire or market need for
it.


- Global demand for renewable energy continues to grow.
- The new transit line should reduce demand for downtown parking.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: access ___ + place, service, information, or resource
column3:
Use the uncountable noun frame access to + NP for the right or ability to
reach or use something.


- Every student should have access to a qualified school counselor.
- The archive provides researchers with **access to previously classified
documents**.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Complete the matched opportunity frames.


1. The fellowship gave Maya an opportunity ___ conduct fieldwork in Kenya.
(the performer is already clear)
2. The online program created an opportunity ___ rural nurses ___ receive
specialist training. (the performer must be named)
column3:
1. The fellowship gave Maya an opportunity to conduct fieldwork in Kenya.
2. The online program created **an opportunity for rural nurses to receive
specialist training**.


Use opportunity to + base verb when the performer is understood from the
sentence. Use opportunity for + NP + to-inf to name the performer
explicitly. A bare opportunity for + activity can also be natural, but it
does not express this actor/action contrast.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: the/an ability ___ + base verb
column3:
Use the/an ability to + base verb for the capacity to perform an action.


- Critical thinking includes **the ability to evaluate conflicting
evidence**.
- The medication may impair a patient's ability to drive safely.


Compare the adjective frame be capable of + V-ing.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
In neutral AmE, retrieve the usual noun frame for a way of thinking or
feeling: attitude ___ + person or issue.
column3:
Use attitude toward + person/issue as the usual neutral AmE frame.


- The survey measured young adults' attitudes toward remote work.
- A manager's attitude toward constructive criticism shapes team culture.


Attitude to is also established, especially in British English and in
some formal contexts.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: an opinion ___ + person or thing being evaluated
column3:
Use an opinion of + person/thing for an evaluation or judgment of that
entity.


- The internship gave Elena a more favorable opinion of the organization.
- Voters' opinion of the mayor improved after the crisis.


For a view on an issue, opinion about or opinion on is often more
natural.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Retrieve the two common noun frames for a view on an issue:
an opinion ___/___ + issue.
column3:
Use an opinion about/on + issue for a view concerning a topic or question.


- Residents expressed strong **opinions about the proposed highway
expansion**.
- The ethics committee has not yet issued **an opinion on the use of facial
recognition**.


About is broadly neutral; on is especially common for formal topics
and positions. The two often overlap.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: confidence ___ + person, institution, ability, or system
column3:
Use confidence in + person/institution/ability/system for trust in its
ability or reliability.


- Public confidence in the judicial system has declined.
- She has complete confidence in her team's ability to meet the deadline.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Which forms are normal, and what does each tend to foreground?


1. concern for/about the displaced families
2. concern about/over the housing shortage
column3:
All four printed forms are normal.


- concern for + person/group can foreground care for welfare.
- concern about + person/issue is a broad worry frame.
- concern over + issue is common, especially in formal reporting.


The meanings overlap, so do not force an exclusive choice from a broad noun
alone.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Complete with between or with.


1. The study examined the relationship ___ housing insecurity and mental
health. (two named variables)
2. The research team strengthened its relationship ___ the community clinic.
(one other participant)
column3:
1. The study examined **the relationship between housing insecurity and
mental health**.
2. The research team strengthened **its relationship with the community
clinic**.


Use relationship between + two or more participants/variables to link them.
Use relationship with + one participant from the subject's perspective.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Give the two common prepositions that can name one other endpoint:


a connection ___/___ + entity, system, person, or topic
column3:
Use a connection with/to + endpoint. Both forms can name the associated
entity; lexical preference and emphasis vary.


- Investigators found no connection with any extremist organization.
- The evidence may have a connection to the earlier complaint.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Complete sentence 1 with between. Give both accepted one-endpoint forms
for sentence 2.


1. Researchers found a strong connection ___ chronic stress and sleep
disruption. (two named phenomena)
2. Investigators found no connection ___/___ the lobbying firm.
(one associated entity)
column3:
1. Researchers found **a strong connection between chronic stress and sleep
disruption**.
2. Investigators found no connection with/to the lobbying firm.


Use connection between + A and B when both sides are named. Use
connection with/to + one endpoint when the other endpoint is named from an
external reference point; with and to often overlap.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: contact ___ + person or group
column3:
Use contact with + person/group for communication or physical interaction
with them.


- The nurse had prolonged contact with an infected patient.
- Regular contact with native speakers can improve listening fluency.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Which completed frames are standard, and what does each structure foreground?


1. a comparison of A with/to B
2. a comparison between A and B
column3:
Both printed frames are standard. Comparison of A with B is a useful
analytical default; to often supports likeness or analogy, but contemporary
usage overlaps. Comparison between A and B explicitly names both compared
sides.


- The report includes **a comparison of current data with data from the
previous decade**.
- The essay makes a comparison of the city to a living organism.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Both forms are standard. What kind of meaning do they share?


1. the advantage of sharing anonymized data
2. the advantage to sharing anonymized data
column3:
Both advantage(s) of + NP/V-ing and advantage(s) to + NP/V-ing can name a
benefit associated with a thing, feature, or activity. Of is a useful broad
production default; the two forms overlap.


- The main advantage of remote consultations is easier access for rural
patients.
- One advantage of sharing anonymized data is that researchers can
replicate the findings.


Recipient frames such as an advantage for students are a separate meaning;
do not infer that to is the only possible recipient connector.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Use the conventional broad default:


a disadvantage ___ + thing, choice, or V-ing
column3:
Use a disadvantage of + thing/choice for a drawback associated with it.


- A major disadvantage of the treatment is its high cost.
- One disadvantage of living far from campus is the lengthy commute.


Also OK in other frames: a disadvantage to choosing this route and
a disadvantage for rural residents.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Match each completed frame to its conventional role.


- the benefits of the policy
- a benefit from the policy
- a benefit to residents
- for residents' benefit
column3:
- benefits of + source associates benefits with the source.
- benefit from + source foregrounds the origin from which it is obtained.
- benefit to + recipient names a helpful effect received by that party.
- for someone's benefit means intended to help that person or group.


These frames form a source-versus-recipient system; broad contexts can overlap.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Match each completed frame to its conventional role.


1. the cost of maintaining the bridge
2. a substantial cost to patients
3. the monthly cost for low-income households
column3:
1. cost of + source/action names the thing or action whose cost is considered.
2. cost to + affected party foregrounds the burden borne by that party.
3. cost for + person/group can name the price or expense applicable to them.


These are conventional emphases, not a claim that to and for never
overlap in recipient contexts.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Complete with for or to.


1. The agency accepts responsibility ___ monitoring water quality.
(the duty)
2. The agency has a responsibility ___ the communities it serves.
(the people to whom the duty is owed)
column3:
1. The agency accepts responsibility for monitoring water quality.
2. The agency has a responsibility to the communities it serves.


Use responsibility for + duty/outcome/V-ing for what someone is responsible
for. Use responsibility to + person/group/authority for whom the duty is
owed.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Match each completed frame to its conventional emphasis, then state the
overlap.


1. control over prices or the outcome
2. control of the organization or system
column3:
Control over often foregrounds power or influence. Control of often
foregrounds possession or management.


- Local authorities have little control over global energy prices.
- The study gave participants greater **control over how their data would be
used**.


The meanings overlap whenever either construal is available, so do not force
one preposition from a broad noun alone.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: a request ___ + thing, information, or assistance
column3:
Use a request for + thing/information/assistance for an ask that seeks it.


- The agency denied a request for access to the raw data.
- We received an urgent request for technical assistance.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: an invitation ___ + event, place, or activity
column3:
Use an invitation to + event/place/activity for an offer to attend or take
part.


- I accepted an invitation to the annual policy forum.
- Each finalist received an invitation to the awards ceremony.


To name an invited performer, an invitation for + NP + to-inf is possible:
an invitation for Dr. Chen to speak.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Give the broad default and the normal goal-oriented alternative:


a contribution ___/___ + result, goal, cause, field, or collection
column3:
Use a contribution to + result/cause/field/collection as the broad default.
Toward is a normal AmE alternative when progress toward a goal or cause is
foregrounded.


- Her research made a substantial contribution to climate science.
- Community donations made a vital contribution toward the relief goal.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
Give the safer broad default and the contemporary allocation-oriented variant:


an investment ___/___ + asset, sector, field, or V-ing activity
column3:
Use an investment in + asset/field/V-ing for money, time, or effort put into
it for future value.


- The city approved a major investment in public transit.
- Mentoring is an investment in developing future leaders.


Investment into + asset/sector also occurs in contemporary business and
policy usage and can foreground directed allocation. Prefer in as the broad
neutral learner default.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2: participation ___ + activity or process
column3:
Use participation in + activity/process for the act of taking part in it.


- Student participation in local elections remains low.
- Active participation in designing the policy increased public trust.

column1: EN::Connection Patterns::04 Noun Patterns
column2:
What does each completed frame foreground?


1. her involvement in drafting the legislation
2. her involvement with a private lobbying group
column3:
1. involvement in + activity/group foregrounds participation or membership.
